mmlab@SIGS \lablockup      \coverwordmarkassets/cover_wordmark.texA Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action,
and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation \affiliations \authornotes \paperabstractEmbodied intelligence aims to enable robots to perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks often evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks, or evaluate them in separate assessments without examining their composition, thus providing limited insight into whether failures arise from reasoning, physical execution, or their composition. To fill this gap, we introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 simulated manipulation tasks across five real-world application domains. Each task features three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. These tasks are organized into three views: Mind emphasizes decisions based on historical observation, Act assesses precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act integrates reasoning and physical execution in closed-loop tasks, where action outcomes guide subsequent decisions. By contrasting performance across the three views, Mind2Act World reveals whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose the capabilities it already has. Furthermore, we develop a diagnosis harness that attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a per-model report called a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem. \paperlinks  Website: mind2act-world.com  Code: Benchmark  Tasks  Leaderboard  Diagnosis  Document  Community

Mind tasks test history-based reasoning, Act tasks test precise and timely physical execution, and Mind2Act tasks test their closed-loop composition, where action outcomes guide subsequent decisions. 1 Introduction

“Knowledge is the beginning of action and action is the completion of knowledge.” — Wang Yangming

The central ambition of embodied intelligence is to enable robots to perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability. Studies of human sensorimotor control indicate that adaptive and reliable manipulation involves reasoning over task-relevant information, executing physical actions precisely, and adapting behavior through environmental feedback [1, 2, 3]. In the cooking task of Fig. , a robot must remember which ingredient to add next, coordinate both arms to add the ingredient, and switch the stove from heating to keep-warm mode based on temperature feedback. These requirements motivate three capabilities. Mind decides what to do from earlier observations. Act produces the required physical effect in time. Mind-Action Composition closes the loop, so that remembered information guides each action and each physical outcome updates the next decision.

Recent embodied systems spanning multimodal agents [32], vision-language-action models (VLAs) [19, 20], world-action models (WAMs) [23, 26], and hybrid architectures [27, 28] have substantially advanced robotic manipulation. However, their capabilities in Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition remain poorly understood, which makes it difficult to identify capability bottlenecks and guide further development. Two limitations of existing embodied benchmarks [4, 6, 7, 8, 12] explain why. First, conventional benchmarks often assess cognitive reasoning and physical execution within the same tasks and report only whether a task succeeds [4, 5, 6], so a failure cannot be traced to Mind or Act. Second, although recent benchmarks have introduced finer-grained diagnostics and separate assessments of reasoning and physical execution [8, 11, 12, 13], they rarely evaluate Mind-Action Composition, particularly whether physical outcomes can effectively inform subsequent decisions. Closing this gap requires tasks that stress one capability while keeping the others present but easy, a judgment of composition based on verified physical outcomes, and a comparison of systems with different action interfaces and inference speeds on equal terms.

To this end, we introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark for Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition in robotic manipulation (Fig. ). Its 30 tasks come from five real-world application domains and are organized into three views of ten tasks each, covering 12 capability categories. Each view emphasizes one demand by design. Mind tasks keep physical operations simple, Act tasks state the required operation explicitly, and Mind2Act tasks chain dependent operations so that each physical outcome decides what comes next. Success is judged from physical predicates on the environment, and the evaluator records stages and events within each episode. Each task has three difficulty levels that raise its demands while keeping the objective fixed. Each level runs in a Clean and a Random scene, which share the same instance but differ in clutter, materials and lighting (180 configurations in total). Agents and end-to-end policies share the same tasks, information contract and evaluator, and 4,500 demonstrations (75.8 hours) are provided for fine-tuning end-to-end policies. A diagnosis harness combines rule-based analysis of the evaluator’s stage and event records with an LLM judge to attribute each failed episode of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition. It summarizes each of these systems in a per-model report called a model profile card (Fig. 5; Appendix E.4).

Our evaluation on Mind2Act World reveals a clear pattern. Existing architectures are uneven across Mind and Act, yet all struggle with Mind-Action Composition. The strongest agent retains task state well but struggles to sustain contact, and its timed successes are measured with a simulator that pauses during inference. End-to-end policies respond within a fraction of a second and execute practiced motions, but retain little task state, and the memory of the VLAs largely disappears under scene randomization. Notably, on Mind2Act, the strongest system succeeds in only 12.0% of episodes, far below its 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act, and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Competence in either capability therefore does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks.

The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 manipulation tasks grounded in real-world requirements. Organized into three views, it systematically evaluates Mind, Act, and Mind-Action Composition.

  • •

    We develop a diagnosis harness that combines rule-based analysis with an LLM judge to identify the stage at which each failed episode first breaks down and to attribute the failure to Mind, Act, or Mind-Action Composition. The harness also summarizes three representative models in model profile cards of their failure patterns and behavioral tendencies.

  • •

    We evaluate representative multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs on shared tasks and scoring, with separate leaderboards for agents and end-to-end policies. Our results show that systems differ in which of Mind and Act is weaker, and that all of them struggle with Mind-Action Composition.

2 Related Work

2.1 Embodied Policies and Agents

Robot manipulation policies have evolved from imitation learning [15, 16, 17] to large-scale generalist policies. Vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA [19], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [20], RDT2 [21] and G0.5 [22] improve instruction following and cross-task transfer, while world-action models such as LDA-1B [24], Motus [25] and DreamZero [26] couple predictive modeling with control. Agent-based systems take a different route, turning language-model reasoning into executable programs [32] and feeding success detection back into planning [67, 68]. Recent work also addresses memory-augmented manipulation [29, 30, 55], dynamic manipulation [61, 62], and force- or tactile-aware control [65, 66].

Despite this progress, each line is usually evaluated where only its own demand is hard: memory methods on tasks with simple execution, dynamic and contact-aware controllers on tasks whose target is given, and agents on tasks where perceiving the outcome is assumed. In practice, a failure may come from holding the wrong task state, missing the intended physical effect, or continuing without checking that the effect occurred. Mind2Act World therefore makes all three demands hard within the same tasks and evaluates agents, VLAs and WAMs on them.

2.2 Evaluation for Manipulation and Embodied Agents

Simulation benchmarks provide scalable testbeds for manipulation. RLBench [5], CALVIN [33] and LIBERO [4] cover multi-task, language-conditioned and lifelong settings. RoboTwin 2.0 [34] evaluates bimanual generalization, and THE COLOSSEUM [48] stresses distribution shift. BEHAVIOR-1K [7] and RoboCasa [6] pose long household activities. Memory benchmarks such as RMBench [31] and RoboMME [38] isolate history-dependent decisions, the latter with Easy, Medium and Hard levels and timed stopping of moving objects. GeoMind [36] evaluates spatial reasoning and spatial memory through structured manipulation tasks, with controlled scene variations and diagnostic metrics for spatial understanding and execution failures. RoboDojo [8] and RobotWorld [9] diagnose capability dimensions with stage scores or execution traces, and real-world benchmarks such as RoboArena [41] assess deployed policies. For agents built on foundation models, EmbodiedBench [52] spans high-level and low-level embodied tasks, and Embodied Playground [11] evaluates closed-loop behavior in which earlier actions set up later prerequisites. X2Real [12] records subtask failure nodes, separates reasoning from manipulation dimensions including dynamic operation, and compares VLA, WAM and agent routes. RoboColiseum [13] reports a gap between task understanding and reliable execution. RLE-Bench [10] and Embodied First Exam [14] instead evaluate agents that write and iterate on code to solve robot control and robot learning engineering problems.

Most of these benchmarks entangle reasoning and execution within one task, so a failure cannot be attributed to either, or measure them in separate evaluations, leaving open whether they hold together when one realized outcome sets the conditions for the next decision. Mind2Act World addresses this gap by deriving tasks from real-world requirements and organizing them into Mind, Act and Mind2Act views with graded difficulty, so that the same demands are measured in isolation and in composition across architectures. Table 1 compares Mind2Act World with 21 representative simulation benchmarks. Mind2Act World tasks also have long horizons, with training demonstrations averaging 60.7 s overall and 99.6 s in the Mind2Act view. Demonstrations in RoboTwin 2.0, RoboDojo, MIKASA-Robo-VLA and RoboCasa365 average 13 to 40 s, and only BEHAVIOR-1K, whose tasks are full household activities, has longer ones.

3 Mind2Act World Benchmark

Mind2Act World asks whether failures in manipulation tasks arise from incorrect reasoning, imprecise execution, or a poor composition of the two. The benchmark comprises 30 simulation tasks on a bimanual ARX X5 platform, organized into 3 views that place different demands on a system. Mind focuses on history-dependent reasoning, Act emphasizes constrained physical execution, and Mind2Act focuses on their composition. Each task has Easy, Medium, and Hard levels, and each level is evaluated in a Clean and a Random scene setting, yielding 180 configurations. Fig. 1 presents an overview of our 30 tasks. The following sections describe the design principles (Section 3.1), task views (Section 3.2), difficulty levels (Section 3.3), training data (Section 3.4), and evaluation setting (Section 3.5).

3.1 Design Principles

Four principles guide the benchmark design: (i) build tasks from real-world requirements, (ii) evaluate reasoning and execution capabilities separately and in combination, (iii) verify physical outcomes and record task progress, and (iv) support evaluation across different model architectures.

(i) Tasks are built from real-world requirements.

Embodied agents in industry, homes, and service settings must follow instructions across multiple stages and produce the required physical effects at the right time. We construct tasks in three steps. First, we identify a practical requirement, such as remembering orders after they leave view, maintaining a target instrument reading, intercepting objects on a conveyor, or responding to appliance feedback. We then reproduce this requirement in a tabletop scene and define completion conditions based on physical outcomes. Table 2 groups the tasks into five application domains: home and food service, manufacturing and logistics, instrument operation and dexterous tool use, assembly and physical reasoning, and companion and edutainment. It also identifies the industrial or service requirement behind each task. In the companion and edutainment domain, structured activities such as card matching and paddle ball represent cognitive and sports training for older adults and children. All thirty tasks are tabletop abstractions of such needs. They isolate the requirement that makes the activity hard for a robot and do not reproduce a deployed workflow in full.

(ii) Capabilities are decoupled, then recoupled.

Long-horizon tasks often combine memory, planning, precision, and timing, making the source of failure difficult to identify. Mind2Act World evaluates these demands through three views with related task semantics. Mind tasks require only routine execution, so they examine how a system maintains and uses task state. Act tasks specify the required operation to examine its physical execution ability. Mind2Act tasks combine these demands and test composition in both directions. Retained task state guides actions, and the physical outcomes of those actions update that state. The views define observable task demands, not internal policy modules. Each view emphasizes one demand without removing the other. A Mind task still requires routine grasping and placing, and an Act task still requires reading the cue that it responds to. Strong performance on the separate demands with weak performance on their combination is therefore consistent with a composition problem. Because the views contain different tasks and Mind2Act workflows are also longer, view-level differences do not by themselves identify composition failures (Section 5.2). Matched interventions are left to future work (Section 7).

(iii) Outcomes are physically verified and traced within the episode.

Task scores depend on simulator states and events. A deposit counts only after an object is released and supported at the target. A dial reading must remain stable after release, and a key strike must produce an effective press. The task records also distinguish incorrect decisions from failed execution, such as selecting the wrong object versus failing to place the correct one. Partial-progress scores and event records show which stages were completed and where the first observable error occurred.

(iv) Evaluation is architecture-agnostic.

The benchmark supports comparisons across architectures using shared tasks, instances, and scoring rules. End-to-end policies act from observations after training on the shared demonstrations; agents act through declared motion tools. Section 4 specifies what each interface exposes, so that differences in performance can be read against differences in information and control.

3.2 Task Design

Task design follows the three views introduced above. Mind tests decisions that depend on earlier information (Section 3.2.1). Act tests whether a specified operation produces the required physical effect within spatial and temporal constraints (Section 3.2.2). Mind2Act tests their composition across dependent operations (Section 3.2.3). Within each view, tasks are grouped by capability. The following subsections explain each category through representative tasks and describe the failures it can reveal. Appendix Table 20 lists all tasks, their source workflows, categories, and difficulty variables. Appendix F provides the full specifications.

3.2.1 Mind: Reasoning over Long-Horizon Dependencies

A decision may depend on information that is no longer visible, such as a part on an earlier tray, the effect of an unlabeled control, or the portion of an order already served. These dependencies require a system to retain evidence and update task state throughout an episode. Many end-to-end visuomotor policies use only the current observation or a short history of recent frames [15, 16, 19, 20]. Recent memory-augmented policies have begun to address this limitation [56, 29, 55, 30]. Mind tasks examine whether a system can make correct decisions after relevant cues disappear, while requiring only routine execution.

Memory categories.

The ten Mind tasks cover five memory categories, with two tasks per category. The categories differ in how earlier information supports later decisions. Entity memory retains an object’s identity or an associated value when its current appearance is insufficient. Feedback-rule learning uses interaction to infer and retain a rule or hidden configuration. Examples include learning the effects of unlabeled controls and recovering an arrangement from feedback that reports only the number of correct positions. Process memory tracks completed operations and their order, such as fulfilled requests or the original order of disassembled layers. Spatial memory retains locations when a reference frame moves or a map is hidden. Integrated memory combines identity, location, and order, as in tracking a covered workpiece or matching cards revealed two at a time. Difficulty increases the information to retain, such as bindings, layers, hazard cells, card pairs, or exchanges, while keeping precision demands low.

Representative cases.

We demonstrate representative cases in Fig. 2. In workpiece tracking and route replay (M1), the robot remembers the target location and station route, tracks the hidden target through cover exchanges, and retrieves it to visit the required stations in order. This tests integrated memory of identity, location, and sequence. In steamer-stack order restoration (P2), the robot observes each basket’s contents as it unstacks the baskets, then restores their original order and replaces the lid. On Hard, distractor baskets have identical exteriors but different contents. The robot must retain the original layer order and select the correct baskets, testing process memory.

What Mind diagnoses.

Mind task records distinguish decision errors from execution errors, such as choosing the wrong item versus failing to place the correct one. Because execution is routine, an error on a Mind task usually comes from the task state a system maintains.

3.2.2 Act: Dynamic Response and Precise Physical Execution

Correct decisions must be translated into physical effects that meet spatial and temporal constraints. Common examples include intercepting conveyor objects, passing through cyclic gates, maintaining instrument readings, carrying loose loads, and folding fabric. Act tasks specify what to do and evaluate how it is executed. Act provides a reference for execution demands that also occur in Mind2Act workflows, such as conveyor pickup in meal assembly. This allows performance on separate operations to be compared with performance in a dependent workflow.

Execution categories.

Dynamic response concerns the timing of an action’s effect relative to a changing scene. Examples include intercepting objects before they leave the reachable region, pressing a button within a cue window, and passing through a cyclic gate before it closes. Dynamic stability adds a related demand. The robot must control its own motion without disturbing a carried load, such as loose balls on a tray. Timing follows the simulation clock, which pauses during inference. Precise physical execution concerns spatial accuracy, contact, and stability. It includes setting instrument readings, maintaining tool contact along a path, controlling stamp orientation, folding cloth that remains flat after release, and spacing dominoes to complete a physical chain to a bell. Difficulty increases through shorter time windows, additional obstacles or loads, tighter tolerances, and less controllable materials or shapes.

Representative cases.

Cases are demonstrated in Fig. 2. In domino chain to a bell (PR6), the robot places dominoes upright along a curved band and pushes the first to trigger a chain that rings a bell. This requires precise spacing and orientation so that contact propagates through the chain. Difficulty increases with more dominoes, greater height variation, and a larger band span. In tray carrying with loose balls (DR4), the robot carries loose balls on a tray past obstacles while keeping each ball within its marked circle. This tests dynamic stability, as the robot must control tray motion to preserve the positions of the balls throughout transport.

What Act diagnoses.

Act tasks assess endpoint accuracy, stability after release, contact continuity, and timing. By limiting long-horizon reasoning demands, they provide a reference for interpreting execution failures in Mind2Act workflows.

3.2.3 Mind2Act: Composition across Dependent Operations

Mind2Act evaluates how reasoning and execution interact across a workflow. Retained information, such as an order, layout, or recipe sequence, determines the next operation and its execution requirements. Each physical outcome then changes the task state on which later decisions depend. A system may handle the separate demands yet struggle to combine them over time. Mind2Act therefore focuses on outcome-conditioned continuation, that is, choosing subsequent actions from the state produced by earlier operations. Each task combines a memory or reasoning demand with a physical execution demand, as listed in Appendix Table 20.

Composition mechanisms.

The tasks cover five composition mechanisms. In cumulative progress (CP01, CP03), remaining demand or slot occupancy determines the next operation. Progress advances only after successful delivery or stable plate placement. In state-dependent prerequisites and repair (CP02, CP08, CP09), later operations require a valid physical state. The robot may need to stop a turntable before covering a cake, rebuild a misplaced base to match a remembered blueprint, or redraw original strokes removed during erasing. In feedback-driven adjustment (CP04, CP06), temperature or balance-beam deflection guides the next operation. In sequence and plan execution (CP05, CP07), a remembered sequence or a construction plan determines the order of operations. Progress requires effective strikes or stable placements; CP07 also requires a toy car to cross the completed bridge. In predictive decision under time pressure (CP10), the robot applies a fixed color rule to each incoming ball: return a white ball and let a red ball pass. It must select and time its response before the ball arrives.

Representative cases.

In rotating-cake decoration (CP02), the robot remembers a briefly shown macaron layout and reproduces it on a rotating cake. It must stop the turntable and verify that the cake is stationary before placing the cover. In temperature-controlled cooking (CP04), the robot adds ingredients in the remembered recipe order, then uses temperature feedback to switch from HEAT to KEEP WARM within the required time window. Bridge building for a toy car (CP07) requires selecting suitable parts and executing a construction plan. The assembled bridge must remain stable after release and support the car as it crosses the gap, linking plan execution to a physical test of the completed structure. In whiteboard restoration (CP09), the robot compares the current board with a remembered drawing to identify added strokes. It must erase these strokes and redraw any original content removed during erasing, so that the final board matches the remembered colors, shapes, and layout.

What Mind2Act diagnoses.

Mind2Act examines whether a system uses retained information to guide execution and updates that information from physical outcomes. Comparisons across views, supported by stage and event records, help identify composition failures.

Difficulty inside the process.

Task difficulty often arises during intermediate operations. Fig. 2 shows four steps from each of eight Hard-level demonstrations, two Mind, two Act and four Mind2Act tasks. At Hard, M1 involves seven cover exchanges, two of them irrelevant, and P2 involves four steamer tiers and two identical decoys. PR6 involves nine dominoes of mixed sizes along a 76 cm curved band, and DR4 involves four loose balls, two pillars and a marked circle of 20 mm radius. CP02 shows its sample for 3 s, CP04 involves bimanual jar handling and a switch from HEAT to KEEP WARM within 2 s of the pot reaching 80 °C, CP07 uses 13 of 28 parts across a 36 cm river, and CP09 requires uncapping pens with both hands. Failures in these intermediate operations can prevent later stages from succeeding, so we report stage progress alongside final success (Section 4.3).

3.3 Difficulty Design

Aggregate scores can obscure the conditions under which performance declines. We therefore define three difficulty levels for each task. The objective remains fixed, while memory load, reasoning demands, precision, timing, or workflow dependencies increase. Easy tests the core requirement under the least demanding conditions. Medium increases the information to retain, the required precision, or the number of operations. Hard introduces greater demands through tighter constraints, longer dependent sequences, or combinations of these factors. The levels define a progression within each task rather than a common numerical scale across tasks. Comparing success and partial-progress scores across the three levels shows how performance on the same task changes as its demands increase. Fig. 3 illustrates these variations. Mind tasks increase the information to retain, such as unknown mappings, blocks, hidden hazards, or card pairs, while requiring only routine execution. Act tasks vary physical demands, including load, path shape, fold geometry, and domino count. Mind2Act tasks vary orders, river width, shapes, or balls to increase the number and dependencies of operations. Appendix F specifies every task and difficulty level.

3.4 Training Data and Collection

To compare end-to-end policies fairly, we provide expert demonstrations collected under one protocol for every task and level. Section 3.4.1 describes how they are generated and checked, and Section 3.4.2 summarizes the resulting data.

3.4.1 Data Collection and Quality Control

Each episode has a setup defined at three levels. The task determines the objective and rules, the difficulty level determines the demands, and episode parameters specify variations such as object positions, orders, or target readings. Task scripts define the operation sequence and end-effector targets. Inverse kinematics and motion planning convert these targets into joint trajectories. Quality control checks physical completion against simulator states and events. For example, CP01 requires the requested items to be released into the correct tray and remain supported. Recording checks cover missing or corrupted frames, invalid state or action values, timestamp alignment, and duplicates. Demonstrations must also satisfy task-specific qualification conditions to provide clear examples for learning. A DR3 demonstration must retain at least one second of withdrawal margin, and an M2 demonstration must use only information revealed by actual card flips. These conditions are stricter than task success requirements and apply to demonstration selection rather than policy scoring. Every retained demonstration passes the evaluator used at test time. The collection therefore also shows that each task and level can be completed on this platform by a scripted controller with access to simulator state. Demonstration and evaluation seeds are disjoint.

3.4.2 Data Statistics

Each episode records the task instruction, RGB images from a head camera and two wrist cameras at 640×480640\times 480, and joint states and targets. Physics runs at 120 Hz, and the recorded data are sampled at 30 Hz. Across the thirty tasks, the dataset contains 50 episodes per task and difficulty level, resulting in 4,500 episodes, 8.19 million frames per camera, and 75.8 hours of recordings, as detailed in Appendix Table 8. Mind and Mind2Act episodes average 58.5 and 99.6 seconds, compared with 23.9 seconds for Act. These averages are approximately 2.5 and 4.2 times the Act average, respectively. Hard Mind2Act episodes average 127.6 seconds.

3.5 Evaluation Setting

Policies are evaluated through closed-loop interaction with the environment. Each episode starts from a predefined test instance, and the system selects actions using updated observations. Execution ends on task completion, task-defined failure, system termination, or budget exhaustion. Each configuration is defined by a task, a difficulty level, and a scene setting. An end-to-end policy runs all 50 instances of each configuration, and an agent runs a shared subset of 5. Instance parameters are fixed in advance and shared across systems within the same evaluation protocol to control variation between runs.

We report two metrics. Final success rate is the fraction of valid episodes that meet all completion conditions. Task score ranges from 0 to 100 and measures partial progress under task-specific rules. High task scores with low final success indicate that a system completes parts of a task but often fails to meet all requirements. This distinction supports analysis of incomplete workflows in Mind2Act. Both metrics are computed from simulator states and events. Invalid or missing runs are recorded separately. Section 4 specifies the interfaces, timing, scoring, and aggregation rules.

3.5.1 Episode Variation and Randomization

Episodes share the same objective, rules, and difficulty level but vary task-specific initial states and parameters. These include object layouts, initial and target states such as end-effector poses, and event sequences such as piano-key order. Some tasks also vary continuous and hidden parameters. In CP10, launcher position and aim are sampled continuously, while the task seed determines the order of red and white balls. In PR5, the target angle is sampled from a set defined for each difficulty level. The sheet displays a target arrow without revealing the numerical angle or tolerance. These variations test whether a system can adapt its behavior rather than replay a memorized trajectory. Using shared test instances supports controlled comparisons. Each task and difficulty level is evaluated in two scene settings, which we treat as separate configurations, giving 180 configurations in total (30 tasks ×\times 3 levels ×\times 2 settings). The Clean setting fixes scene appearance. The Random setting uses the same task instances and additionally varies clutter, table and floor materials, and lighting as depicted in Fig. 4. Because the two settings share task instances, comparing them isolates the effect of visual and scene perturbation from that of task demands. Appendix A.4 details how the two settings are generated.

4 Technical Implementation and Evaluation Protocol

Systems that act through different interfaces must face the same scenes, the same clock and the same notion of success. Building on the task design in Section 3, this section describes how policies connect to the tasks, how an episode is executed and timed, and how its outcome is scored and protected against shortcuts. Appendix B collects the implementation details needed for reproduction.

4.1 Platform and Policy Interfaces

Comparing agents and end-to-end policies requires a platform that both can drive and that produces the same physical effects for both. We implement Mind2Act World in Isaac Sim with two ARX X5 arms and parallel grippers. A fixed head camera captures the scene layout, while two wrist cameras capture local gripper-object interactions. RGB images are rendered at 640×480640\times 480 for all cameras. Task scenes combine shared robot and workspace assets with task-specific objects and mechanisms as depicted in Fig. 6. Their geometry, motion, and contact properties are configured to reproduce the physical effects required by each task.

All systems follow a common information contract detailed in Appendix B. Policies receive the task instruction, selected RGB views, and declared robot state. History access is limited to information previously exposed within the same episode. Hidden simulator state is accessible only to the evaluator. This includes unannounced parameters used for scoring, such as the numerical target angle and tolerance in PR5, gate timing in DR3, and allowable ball drift in DR4.

The benchmark supports two action interfaces. End-to-end policies predict joint or end-effector actions. These predictions are converted to joint targets, and a configured number of actions is executed from each chunk before the next prediction. Agents are multimodal language models that issue structured tool calls. The move_eef tool accepts an end-effector pose target and gripper command. The backend handles inverse kinematics and motion planning. The wait_steps tool advances simulation while maintaining the current arm and gripper targets. Agents can use memory_resolve to retrieve a previously observed image by its observation identifier and add it to the model’s context. Retrieval does not advance simulation. An agent can also call give_up to end the episode itself. Every evaluated agent uses this one fixed harness of tools, planner and history access. The same two interfaces cover every task interaction, including count-only feedback (F2), an unnumbered needle gauge (CP06), unnumbered buttons (M2), keypad input (E2), bimanual uncapping (CP09), and tray carrying with loose balls (DR4). No task requires a task-specific interface.

4.2 Episode Protocol and Timing

Each episode starts from a fixed instance for its task, difficulty level and scene setting, and systems evaluated under the same protocol use the same instance list. Reset restores the robot, objects, task stage, evaluator, and random-number state. Policy memory is cleared between episodes and retained across stages within an episode. Physics simulation advances at 120 Hz, while arm and gripper targets are updated at 30 Hz. Simulation pauses during model inference. Task deadlines use simulation time, while inference latency and total runtime use wall-clock time, the elapsed real time. A delayed model response therefore consumes wall-clock time without reducing the simulated response window, so timed tasks measure responses in simulation time rather than real-time performance. For end-to-end policies, each task and difficulty level has an episode horizon set to 1.2 times the 90th percentile of demonstration durations, rounded up to a control step. These simulation-time limits range from 16.27–420.50 s for Mind, 6.27–156.47 s for Act, and 34.40–308.50 s for Mind2Act. Agents receive four times this physics budget and at most 150 decisions per episode, since a tool call spans many control steps. Wall-clock limits are safety stops, not task limits. An episode stopped by one is scored like any other unfinished episode. Episodes end on completion, policy termination, or budget exhaustion. Simulator crashes and incomplete records are not counted as task failures, and infrastructure aborts are rerun. Appendices A and B specify episode horizons, model-call budgets, and scheduling.

4.3 Metrics and Aggregation

A success rate alone says how often a task is finished but not how far a failed episode got, while a progress score alone can reward work that never completes the task. We therefore report the final success rate (SR), where success requires the complete task predicate, together with a 0–100 task score that credits task-specific progress and equals 100 exactly when the episode succeeds. Partial credit never overrides an unmet terminal requirement. For a task, level and system with NN eligible attempts and outcomes si∈{0,1}s_{i}\in\{0,1\}, the success rate is

S^=1N​∑i=1Nsi,\hat{S}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}, (1)

with protocol timeouts counted as failures and infrastructure aborts rerun. View summaries average the ten tasks of a view, each pooled over its three levels, and the primary result averages the Clean and Random settings. A robot is useful when it completes whole workflows, and in such workflows remembered information and physical execution depend on each other, so strength in either capability alone is not enough. For this reason, the Overall score weights the views as 0.250.25\,Mind+ 0.25\,+\,0.25\,Act+ 0.50\,+\,0.50\,Mind2Act, so that Mind2Act counts as much as the two single views together. The Overall SR is the plain fraction of successful episodes. A Mind2Act task is scored as a whole. Which side failed is assigned by the episode-level diagnosis (Section 6). Partial-credit rules are task-specific, so scores are comparable across systems on one task. For success rates we report 95% Wilson score intervals over episodes, which capture sampling over the fixed instance lists rather than variation between tasks or repeated runs. As a descriptive reference for composition, we also compare a system’s Mind2Act success rate with the product of its Mind and Act success rates, the value expected if a Mind2Act workflow required one independent success of each kind. The task score is defined in Appendix B.3, and per-task success predicates are listed in Appendix F.2.

4.4 Evaluation Integrity

Because an agent can declare that it has finished and a policy can repeat an action until something happens, the evaluator has to judge outcomes. Completion is therefore assessed using environment-side predicates. Commands and success declarations receive credit only when the required physical conditions are met. Repeating an action earns credit only when it satisfies a new requirement. Task rules distinguish irreversible failures, unscored actions, and valid exploration. For example, in DR4, a ball leaving its circle causes failure even if it later rolls back. In F2, submitting an incomplete layout does not consume an attempt. In M2, revealing a mismatched pair is valid exploration. Any action sequence that satisfies the task rules is valid. A run is classified as a valid failure only when its record is sufficient to evaluate the final success conditions. Unavailable observations and infrastructure interruptions are recorded separately.

5 Benchmark Results

Building on the protocol in Section 4, we evaluate nine systems that span the two main routes to embodied manipulation: multimodal agents that act through tools and end-to-end policies trained on demonstrations. Section 5.1 describes the systems and the evaluation procedure. Section 5.2 analyzes how well they reason, act and compose the two, where and why they fall short across views, conditions and application domains, and what the evaluation costs in time and money. Section 5.3 summarizes which system suits which task.

5.1 Experimental Setup

5.1.1 Systems

We evaluate two system families, each ranked on its own leaderboard. Agents are multimodal language models that select motion tools from camera images and robot state, without any training on Mind2Act World. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra [70], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [71] and Gemini-4-Argon [72]. End-to-end policies map observations and the instruction to robot actions after fine-tuning on the shared demonstrations. We evaluate the VLAs KinRT [73], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [20], G0.5 [22] and X-VLA [74], and the WAMs InternW0 [76] and FastWAM [75]. Appendix C lists the evaluated systems.

5.1.2 Training and Adaptation

We fine-tune each end-to-end policy from its public checkpoint on the shared collection of 4,500 demonstrations, fifty per task and difficulty level (Section 3.4.2), with the initialization, global batch size, and training steps of each system detailed in Appendix C. In contrast, we use the agents directly as provided through their APIs, without fine-tuning.

5.1.3 Inference and Evaluation Instances

All evaluations run at 120 Hz physics and 30 Hz control/RGB observations, with simulation paused during inference so that task deadlines are measured in simulation time and inference cost in wall-clock time. Across the 180 configurations (30 tasks ×\times 3 levels ×\times 2 settings), the nine evaluated systems account for 56,700 scored episodes.

At the start of an episode, each system receives the English task instruction, selected camera views, and declared robot state. End-to-end policies generate action chunks that are converted to robot targets at 30 Hz, whereas agents issue pose-level motion-tool requests and may retrieve earlier observations from the same episode. For each task and difficulty level, we fix a shared list of 50 instances and evaluate them in both Clean and Random settings (Table 3). End-to-end policies run on all 100 resulting episodes per task and level (9,000 episodes per policy), while agents run on a shared subset of 5 Clean and 5 Random episodes (900 episodes per agent).

Random instances preserve the underlying task instance while adding table clutter, one of 23 table materials, and one of six light types (with RGB channels scaled in [0,2][0,2] and intensity in [0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2]). The range is deliberately wide, so Random serves as an appearance stress test. End-to-end policies are allotted a simulation-time horizon of 1.2×1.2\times the 90th percentile of demonstration durations, shared across Clean and Random, with a 2-hour wall-clock safety limit. Agents receive 4×4\times this physics budget, up to 150 decisions per episode, and a 6-hour wall-clock safety limit. All three agents are evaluated at medium reasoning effort. Appendix B details the remaining run settings.

5.1.4 Metrics and Statistical Reporting

Following Section 4.3, we report the final success rate (SR) and partial-progress task score (0–100), aggregated across difficulty levels and averaged equally over Clean and Random settings. Alongside point estimates, we provide 95% Wilson score intervals in Appendix D.

5.2 Main Results and Analysis

A failure can come from forgetting task state, failing to execute, or failing to connect the two. We first ask how well current systems reason, act and compose the two, taken as a whole (  OVERALL). We then look at the two capabilities apart before putting them together.  MIND asks whether a system can remember what it has seen.  ACT asks whether it can act precisely and on time.  MIND2ACT asks whether the two still work together inside one workflow.  APPEARANCE changes how the scene looks, and  DIFFICULTY makes the task harder. The last two look beyond the simulator.  LATENCY & COST asks whether a system would keep up in real time, and what the evaluation costs.  REAL WORLD reads the results by application domain and asks how far each is from deployment. Table 5 lists the success rate of every system on each task, grouped by application domain, and Appendix E.2 gives the full episode counts.

OVERALL  How well do current systems reason, act and compose the two?

Current systems can perform single skills but rarely combine them. Table 4 ranks agents and end-to-end policies on separate leaderboards because the two families are evaluated under different settings (Section 5.1). On both leaderboards, the leading systems succeed in only a minority of episodes, with 34.6% for GPT-6 Astra among the agents and 8.7% for InternW0 among the end-to-end policies. The remaining seven systems stay between 2.9% and 7.0%, far below either leader. These low rates are not explained by the tasks themselves, because under the same evaluator a scripted controller with access to simulator state completes every task at every level (Section 3.4.1). Nor is the agent harness the only limit, since the three agents share one harness and GPT-6 Astra still succeeds more than five times as often as the next agent. The shortfall therefore most likely lies in the models themselves.

This progress is also narrow, as Mind and Act tasks, each of which tests a single capability, supply between 81% and 100% of the successes of every system. Within these tasks, the successes cluster on a few practiced motions. Gate passage (DR3) is the clearest case, as this single timed task supplies between 36% and 41% of all successes of KinRT, π0.5\pi_{0.5} and X-VLA and about 70% of those of FastWAM. At the other extreme, eight of the thirty tasks (M1, DR4, PR5, PR6, CP03, CP04, CP07 and CP09) are completed by no system in any of the 56,700 episodes.

The overall ranking hides this, because a system can lead it on single skills alone. For example, InternW0 leads the end-to-end leaderboard because of its Mind and Act results, yet its Mind2Act success rate (3.0%) is below that of π0.5\pi_{0.5} (3.6%). The per-view results show that the two families fail in different ways, as the strongest agent retains task state but struggles to sustain contact, whereas the end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. Both families break down once the two capabilities must work together in one workflow. The VLAs also lose much of their memory when the scene looks different, and Mind2Act workflows collapse most steeply as the difficulty rises.

MIND  Can it remember what it has seen?

Agents can remember what they have seen and end-to-end policies seldom can, but no system reliably keeps track of objects that are moved. The Mind view asks a system to decide what to do from earlier observations, such as an item seen before, a rule learned from feedback, a layout, or the order of earlier operations. On this view, GPT-6 Astra leads by its widest margin and succeeds in 52.7% of Mind episodes (Table 4). By comparison, the other two agents reach only 11.0% and 4.3%, and the end-to-end policies stay between 0.9% and 5.4%. Even these few successes of the end-to-end policies come mostly at Easy, where there is least to remember, so these policies retain little task state of any kind.

However, GPT-6 Astra does not remember equally well on every Mind task. It solves hidden-hazard navigation (S2) in every episode and card matching (M2) in 93%, and it also does well on button mapping (F1, 77%) and repeated-item recognition (E1, 73%). In all four tasks, what the agent remembers stays fixed once seen, and the agent uses it through button presses or simple placements. In contrast, the agent completes no episode of workpiece tracking (M1) or steamer-stack restoration (P2), and M1 remains unsolved by every system. Unlike the other four, these two tasks move the objects that the agent must remember. In M1 the covers are swapped while they hide the workpiece, and in P2 the baskets are unstacked and must be restacked in their original order. As a result, the agent must keep identities, positions and orders up to date while the robot itself lifts and moves the objects. Retrieving its earlier observations does not help here, because a stored image no longer shows where a swapped cover or a moved basket now is.

P2 is also the only Mind task on which the end-to-end policies outperform all three agents, as four of the six policies complete some episodes and KinRT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} reach 15% and 14%. Because these policies retain little task state on the other Mind tasks, their P2 successes more likely come from practiced handling of the baskets than from memory. This also suggests that handling, and not memory alone, limits the agent on P2.

ACT  Can it execute precisely and on time?

End-to-end policies act on time and the strongest agent also acts precisely, but neither family sustains control through contact. The Act view isolates physical execution, since each task states what to do and success depends on doing it precisely and on time. Every end-to-end policy performs best on this view, where the four VLAs reach 12.0 to 19.6% (Table 4), but GPT-6 Astra still leads at 39.0%. For the VLAs, timing is much easier than precision, as on average they succeed in 22 to 28% of the episodes on the four dynamic tasks but in only 4 to 18% on the six precision tasks.

GPT-6 Astra succeeds where the target can be read from the scene and reached in a few deliberate moves. It completes every resistance-adjustment episode (PR1) and 77 to 90% of the episodes on the three timed tasks DR1 to DR3, and it also reaches 43% on voltage setting (PR2), on which no end-to-end policy exceeds 3%. The end-to-end policies, by contrast, succeed where one practiced motion fits the task. On gate passage (DR3), KinRT, π0.5\pi_{0.5} and X-VLA succeed in 76 to 79% of episodes, close to the agent’s 80%, and X-VLA folds the cloth (PR4) in 64% of episodes, where the agent never succeeds.

Both kinds of success break down once a task requires sustained control, meaning that the robot must keep adjusting while it stays in contact with an object. Tasks such as DR4, PR3 and PR6 demand such control, because every small slip changes the state that the next motion must respond to. GPT-6 Astra completes none of the five tasks of this kind (DR4, PR3, PR4, PR5 and PR6), and its profile card shows that the failures occur during the contact itself (Appendix E.4). All 30 of its DR4 episodes are lost while the tray is lifted, and 21 of its 30 PR6 episodes end with dominoes knocked over during placement. Apart from PR4, which one practiced fold can cover, the end-to-end policies fare no better, and no system completes DR4, PR5 or PR6 in any of the 56,700 episodes. These failures point to missing correction during contact rather than to a misunderstanding of the task. Both families execute open-loop between observations, as the agent’s motion tools turn each target into a complete planned trajectory and each end-to-end policy executes a fixed number of actions from each chunk before predicting again (Appendix B). A ball that starts to roll or a domino that starts to tip therefore goes uncorrected until the next observation.

MIND2ACT  Do reasoning and execution work together?

Mind2Act workflows mostly end at their first steps, before reasoning and execution ever have to work together. The Mind2Act view chains dependent operations into one workflow, in which remembered information guides each action and each physical outcome decides what comes next. Table 4 and Fig. 7a show that every system succeeds less often on this view than on Act. GPT-6 Astra drops from 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act to 12.0% on Mind2Act, while the other two agents complete no Mind2Act episode. The end-to-end policies reach only 0.2 to 3.6%, close to their Mind rates and far below their Act rates. For example, X-VLA, the strongest VLA on Act, drops from 19.6% to 0.2%. This shows that strength on a single view does not carry over to workflows that need both, and that for the end-to-end policies the missing memory, rather than execution, sets the limit.

The few Mind2Act successes come from workflows that a system can finish with steps it already performs on the single views. GPT-6 Astra succeeds reliably only on conveyor meal assembly (CP01), in 60% of its episodes, and the picks in CP01 resemble the conveyor pickup of DR1, on which it succeeds in 77%. CP01 alone supplies 18 of its 36 Mind2Act successes, whereas the agent completes no episode of CP03, CP04, CP07, CP09 or CP10. The end-to-end policies, by contrast, succeed mostly at Easy, where a single order or item turns the workflow into little more than an Act task. For KinRT, π0.5\pi_{0.5} and G0.5, produce weighing (CP06) and CP01 supply 81 to 88% of all Mind2Act successes, and π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeeds in 8.6% of its Mind2Act episodes at Easy but in only 0.1% at Hard. These successes therefore reflect practiced steps rather than reasoning and execution working together.

Partial scores further indicate that most Mind2Act episodes fail early rather than near completion. For every system, the Mind2Act score exceeds the success rate by at most 1.5 points, and on CP07 and CP09 no system reaches even the first scored stage. For example, G0.5 never grasps a piece in 202 of its 300 CP07 episodes (Appendix E.4). Errors in the composition itself appear only when an episode gets that far, as when InternW0 switches on the heat before all ingredients are in the pot in 271 of its 300 CP04 episodes. This suggests that Mind2Act failures are driven less by the coordination of reasoning and execution than by single steps that reasoning or execution gets wrong. Reliable composition therefore first requires each capability to hold up at every step of a workflow, which no current system achieves.

APPEARANCE  Does it hold up when the scene looks different?

A change of appearance leaves the strongest agent’s memory largely intact, whereas the VLAs lose most of theirs. The Clean and Random settings use the same task instances, and Random only adds clutter and changes the table materials and the lighting, so comparing the two shows how much a change of appearance alone affects each system. Because all demonstrations were recorded in Clean scenes, Random scenes also look different from what the end-to-end policies saw in training. In overall score the change matters little, since no system gains or loses more than about three points (Appendix Table 11).

The four fine-tuned VLAs, however, keep most of their Act successes and lose most of their Mind successes. They still complete 86 to 94% as many Act episodes in Random scenes as in Clean scenes, but only 28 to 41% as many Mind episodes (Fig. 7b). Their Mind successes fall from 97 to 35 for KinRT, from 82 to 23 for π0.5\pi_{0.5}, from 41 to 17 for G0.5 and from 24 to 7 for X-VLA. An Act task shows its target in the current image, so the policy can still find it among new clutter and lighting. A Mind task instead requires the policy to decide from earlier observations, and in Random scenes those observations look unlike the demonstrations it was trained on. The VLAs therefore seem to remember how a scene looked in training rather than what it contained.

GPT-6 Astra behaves the other way round, as its Mind success rate only moves from 54.7% to 50.7% and its Mind2Act rate stays at 12.0%. It appears to remember what the scene contains, such as which items it has seen and where they are, and new textures, lighting and clutter do not change that. Its Act successes drop more, from 65 to 52 of 150, so for the agent a new appearance hurts execution more than memory. The two world-action models differ from each other, as InternW0 completes 83 Mind episodes in Random against 78 in Clean and keeps 93% of its Act successes, whereas FastWAM falls from 198 to 67 successes overall. For the world-action models, coping with a new appearance therefore depends on the individual model rather than on the model type.

DIFFICULTY  Does it hold up when the task gets harder?

Harder levels hurt most where they add dependent operations, so Mind2Act workflows collapse while timed Act tasks barely change. Each harder level keeps the goal of a task and raises the demand its view is built around (Section 3.3), so Mind tasks give more earlier observations to decide from, Act tasks require more precise or timely execution, and Mind2Act tasks chain more dependent operations. Under these heavier demands every system succeeds less often, but four of the six end-to-end policies lose far more than the strongest agent. Over all tasks, GPT-6 Astra keeps 60% of its success rate from Easy to Hard, falling from 44.7% to 27.0%, whereas KinRT, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, G0.5 and InternW0 keep only 26 to 34%.

This loss is not spread evenly across the views but concentrates where a harder level adds dependent operations. GPT-6 Astra falls from 64% to 44% on Mind and from 44% to 34% on Act, but from 26% to 3% on Mind2Act. This order follows the average length of the demonstrations, which is 23.9 seconds on Act, 58.5 seconds on Mind and 99.6 seconds on Mind2Act (Section 3.4.2). Longer tasks contain more operations that can fail, and each harder Mind2Act level adds more orders, shapes or balls, so a workflow fails as soon as one added operation fails. The end-to-end policies follow the same pattern, with Act holding up best. For example, InternW0 falls from 13.5% to 0.5% on Mind and from 8.0% to 0.3% on Mind2Act but still reaches 12.7% on Act at Hard. Robustness to appearance does not protect against this loss, as InternW0’s Mind rate and GPT-6 Astra’s Mind2Act rate barely change between Clean and Random but fall to 0.5% and 3% at Hard.

The timed Act tasks behave differently, because their harder levels mainly shorten the time in which the physical effect must happen. In DR2 the time allowed to press a lit button drops from 4.0 to 2.6 seconds, yet G0.5 still succeeds in 37, 39 and 34 of 100 episodes at the three levels. DR3 behaves the same way, as the gates stay open for less time while π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeeds in 76, 81 and 79 (Appendix Table 14). A policy with a practiced motion can simply perform it faster, and less time adds no operation that could go wrong. On the precision tasks, success can even depend on the fold a level asks for more than on its difficulty. X-VLA folds the cloth (PR4) in 97 Easy, 1 Medium and 94 Hard episodes of 100, so its learned motion seems to suit the rectangle and hexagon folds but not the diagonal fold of Medium. Harder levels therefore hurt most when they add dependent operations and much less when they mainly shorten the time.

LATENCY & COST  Would it keep up in real time, and what does each success cost?

Agent episodes take longer and cost more as the workflow grows, while end-to-end policies respond within a fraction of a second. Simulation pauses while a model computes, so a timed task measures whether the right action is chosen and executed, not whether it is chosen in time. The pause hides a speed gap of one to nearly three orders of magnitude. As shown in Table 6, an agent call takes 11.0 to 35.6 s, whereas an end-to-end policy takes 77.1 to 488.1 ms, and model requests fill 67 to 86% of an agent episode’s wall-clock time, against 2 to 29% for the end-to-end policies.

For an agent, this time goes to deliberation and grows with how much a task leaves to be decided. GPT-6 Astra spends 16.8 minutes on an Act episode and 19.1 on a Mind episode, but 30.7 on a Mind2Act episode, where each physical outcome changes the next decision and its calls take longest (13.0 s against 9.2 s on Act), yet it completes only 12.0% of these workflows. A longer run does not by itself bring more success, as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is the slowest agent (96.1 minutes per episode) but completes only 6.6% of its episodes, against 34.6% for GPT-6 Astra. GPT-6 Astra, in turn, costs about twenty times as much per episode as the other two agents (USD 25.13 against USD 1.12 to 1.24 at list price), but because it succeeds far more often, its cost per success (USD 72.7) is only about four times that of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (USD 18.9).

End-to-end policies are much faster, and X-VLA, for example, predicts in 153 ms, about seventy times faster than a GPT-6 Astra call. It finishes an Act episode in 6.5 rather than 16.8 minutes and reaches 19.6% on Act, the highest among end-to-end policies and half the agent’s 39.0%. Speed also varies among the end-to-end policies, as InternW0 succeeds slightly more often than KinRT (8.7% against 7.0%) but needs 19.2 rather than 4.8 minutes per episode. The agent’s lead on timed tasks depends on the paused clock, because many of GPT-6 Astra’s Act successes come from conveyor pickup (DR1, 77%) and light-cued response (DR2, 90%), while its mean request time on Act tasks (9.2 s) is more than three times the 2.6 s response window of the Hard light-cued task. In a real setting, the conveyor would keep moving and the light keep changing during that time.

REAL WORLD  How far is each application domain from deployment?

Domains built on pressing and placing reach at best about half of episodes, and kitchens and assembly remain far from deployment. Each task is built from a need in one of five application domains (Table 2), so the per-task results can also be read by domain (Mean rows of Table 5). GPT-6 Astra succeeds in 53.3% of the companion and edutainment episodes and in 46.0% and 42.6% of those in manufacturing and logistics and in instrument and tool use, whose tasks mostly come down to pressing buttons, setting a slider or placing an item. It falls to 17.9% in home and food service and to 4.4% in assembly, where at least half of the tasks are Mind2Act workflows.

The end-to-end policies rank the domains differently, as they do best in manufacturing and logistics (KinRT 20.9%), where conveyor pickup and gate passage repeat one practiced motion, and stay below 12% in every other domain. Four of the five domains each hold two tasks that no system completes, namely kitchen loading and cooking (CP03, CP04), workpiece tracking and tray carrying (M1, DR4), oriented stamping and whiteboard restoration (PR5, CP09), and the domino chain and bridge building (PR6, CP07).

The best domain value, 53.3%, still means failing about every second attempt, so no domain is yet close to deployment even in simulation. Agents come closest in edutainment and manufacturing, end-to-end policies come closest in repetitive factory motions, and neither comes close in kitchens or assembly.

5.3 Which System Suits Which Task

The leaderboards and the analysis of Section 5.2 show how the systems rank and where each of them succeeds and fails. Together they show that agents and end-to-end policies currently handle different kinds of task demand.

Agents for reasoning-heavy steps.

A strong agent is suited to the steps of a task that turn on what was seen before and on what to do next. GPT-6 Astra remembers and reasons well (52.7% on Mind), keeps that memory when the scene changes, and solves tasks whose target can be read and reached in a few deliberate moves. Its limits lie in contact and timing. It completes none of the five contact-rich tasks, and its timed successes are measured with a simulator that waits for it. The other two agents use the same tools yet differ widely on Mind, so this profile is specific to the model.

End-to-end policies for execution-heavy steps.

End-to-end policies are suited to steps that one practiced motion can cover. The four evaluated VLAs retain 86–94% of their Act successes under scene randomization, and each has its own strength: G0.5 on timed reactions, X-VLA on resistance adjustment and cloth folding, and KinRT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on memory, where the VLAs show little. They retain almost no task state, so any step that depends on earlier information is better left to another system.

World-action models differ widely.

InternW0 is the only end-to-end policy whose memory survives scene changes, and it nearly matches the agent on the blueprint task. It still follows its learned sequence without checking preconditions, as in cooking. FastWAM drops in both views under scene randomization, so this advantage is not inherent to world-action models.

Some demands are met by no system yet. No evaluated system succeeds on M1, and GPT-6 Astra completes no episode of P2. No system sustains contact under force (DR4, PR5 and PR6 are never completed), and none completes Mind2Act workflows reliably. GPT-6 Astra reaches 12.0% on Mind2Act, and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Neither family yet covers both reasoning and execution.

6 Diagnostic Analysis

Success rates measure task completion, and task scores measure partial progress. But they cannot identify where or why a system fails within an episode, which is what model developers need to know. In this section, we examine where tasks fail, which errors recur across systems, and how these findings inform improvement priorities. Episode-level diagnosis and model profile cards (Section 6.1) connect failure patterns to task progress, budget use, and stopping decisions (Section 6.2), and the failure codes point to directions for improvement (Section 6.3). Inference latency, runtime and API cost are analyzed alongside success rates in Section 5.2.

6.1 Diagnosis Harness and Model Profile Cards

Diagnosis harness design.

We classify failures by the first unrecoverable error identified in the episode, using 21 failure codes (Appendix E.1). Mind errors concern perception and task reasoning, Act errors concern physical execution, and composition errors concern using physical outcomes to guide subsequent actions. Three episode-level codes capture timeouts, stalls, and cases with insufficient evidence. The label follows the observed error, regardless of the task’s view. A Mind failure involves an error in perception or task reasoning. Examples include selecting the wrong object based on a misremembered order (M-MEMORY) and incorrectly predicting how the scene will change (M-PREDICT). An Act failure occurs when the system selects an appropriate action but executes it incorrectly. Examples include losing a grasp (A-GRASP) and executing the correct action too early or too late (A-TIMING). A composition failure occurs when the system proceeds without verifying a required outcome or fails to update its next action based on feedback. For example, the system may continue pressing the same button after the light cue changes (C-NO-UPDATE).

The harness combines three layers of review as in Fig. 8a. First, deterministic rules use scorer outputs and simulator events to isolate the failure or bound the step at which it occurred. For cases left open by rules, an LLM judge inspects the video and action or tool-call history without overturning rule-based verdicts, flagging ambiguous cases as uncertain. Finally, human reviewers settle the cases the judge marks as uncertain. Fig. 8 shows the workflow on an illustrative example, and Appendix E.4 reports the results of this procedure for every failed episode of three representative systems.

Model profile cards.

A model profile card summarizes the failure profile of a single system. Fig. 8 walks through the diagnosis of an illustrative end-to-end policy, and Fig. 9 shows the full card format with illustrative numbers. The cards of three representative evaluated systems are given in Appendix E.4.

6.2 Failure Patterns of the Evaluated Systems

We read the measured cards of G0.5, InternW0 and GPT-6 Astra (Appendix E.4), together with the run logs of the agents.

The overall pattern.

Physical execution is the largest diagnosed failure group in all three systems, accounting for 41.4% of G0.5’s failures, 37.2% of InternW0’s, and 55.3% of GPT-6 Astra’s. GPT-6 Astra’s failures are particularly concentrated in execution, whereas G0.5 and InternW0 also show substantial perception and reasoning failures, at 27.7% and 32.8%, respectively; 6–11% of each system’s failures occur while closing the loop. These proportions refer to the first unrecoverable error identified in each failed episode. The rule layer alone would overstate Mind-side errors for the end-to-end policies (Appendix Table 17), because scorer records reveal a misremembered item more readily than video reveals a motor fault. A card therefore combines the layers.

The dominant execution errors differ across systems. Failed or lost grasps are the most frequent errors for G0.5 and GPT-6 Astra, with 1,324 and 120 cases, while fine-control errors lead InternW0’s profile with 1,132 cases. The two end-to-end policies also record 924 and 1,011 memory failures. These profiles identify distinct priorities: grasp reliability for G0.5 and GPT-6 Astra, fine control for InternW0, and task-state retention for both end-to-end policies.

Differences across tasks.

The dominant failure also varies by task, even within the same system. For G0.5, 202 of 300 bridge-building episodes (CP07) fail to grasp a construction piece (Fig. 12), making object acquisition the main obstacle to further progress. In light-cued pressing (DR2), however, 90 of 190 failures involve a misread light (M-PERCEIVE) and 88 involve a response that is not updated after the light changes (C-NO-UPDATE). Only eight concern the press itself or its timing. In incremental meal orders (P1), memory errors account for 210 of G0.5’s 300 failed episodes and 245 of InternW0’s 298 failed episodes.

Where progress stops.

No evaluated system completes whiteboard restoration (CP09) or bridge building (CP07), and failures on such workflows often occur before their reasoning stages are reached. On CP09, 299 of 300 G0.5 episodes stop before board removal. GPT-6 Astra fails during the lift in all 30 tray-carrying (DR4) episodes (Fig. 14). Zero success on these tasks is therefore consistent with early physical bottlenecks rather than failures in downstream planning or repair. Most episodes fail in Mind or Act before closed-loop composition is tested.

Analysis of budget use.

Under the same decision budget, the agent logs show distinct termination patterns (Appendix Table 18). Gemini-4-Argon voluntarily stops in 829 of 900 episodes and uses approximately 33 decisions per episode. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses 111.8 decisions on average, voluntarily stops in 385 episodes, and exhausts the decision and physics budgets in 286 and 94 episodes, respectively. GPT-6 Astra averages 79.6 decisions per episode. It voluntarily stops in 460 episodes, and only one of them succeeds, a gate-passage episode (DR3) whose task was already complete when it stopped. The other 459 account for 77.9% of its 589 failed episodes, and in 264 of them the agent has used no more than 100 of the 150 allowed decisions. Among these 459 stops, the first unrecoverable error is attributed to execution in 289 cases, perception or reasoning in 127, and composition in 28. The remaining 15 cases fall outside these three capability groups.

These results distinguish resource limits from the errors that prevent task completion. DeepSeek frequently exhausts its budget. GPT-6 Astra shows a different pattern: many unsuccessful episodes end with substantial decision budget remaining, and execution errors dominate its voluntary stops, often after its motion planner rejects the requested poses. For episodes affected by execution errors, additional decisions are useful only if they enable effective retries or corrective actions (Table 7).

6.3 From Failure Codes to Directions

A diagnosis helps a model developer only if it says what to change, and the profiles narrow broad improvement goals to specific behaviors. Because each failure code names the step and the side of the loop at which an episode broke, a group of codes points to the capability that most needs to improve. An evaluation speaks most directly to two levers that a developer can adjust without redesigning the model. One is the training data of an end-to-end policy. The other is the harness of an agent, that is, the tools and control loop through which it acts. Table 7 maps the three groups of the profile card, and the breakpoints shared by all of them, to such directions. The paragraphs below give the evidence behind each.

Mind failures: task state across stages.

Misremembered information is the most frequent Mind-side code of both measured end-to-end policies, with 924 failures of G0.5 and 1,011 of InternW0, and the VLAs lose 59–72% of their Mind successes when the scene is randomized (Section 5.2). These failures point to maintaining task-relevant identities, order, and progress across operations, and to recognizing an item under a new appearance. Closing this gap calls for data that stress what the failures expose, with varied scene appearance and longer gaps between the moment information is shown and the moment it is needed.

Act failures: grasp, contact and timing.

Failed or lost grasps account for 1,324 failures of G0.5 and fine-control errors for 1,132 of InternW0. On bridge building (CP07), 202 of 300 G0.5 episodes never grasp a piece. G0.5’s frequent grasp failures motivate training and control changes that improve contact acquisition and object retention. InternW0’s fine-control errors motivate closer examination of action resolution and feedback during manipulation. Responses must also fall within the short windows of timed tasks such as the light-cued button (DR2) and the cyclic gates (DR3). On DR3, most failures of the two end-to-end policies come from the withdrawal after delivery rather than from the gate timing. The arm is still inside the gate corridor when the gate closes, or touches the gate while it closes. Demonstrations can be weighted toward these segments, with more variation in object pose, contact and timing, instead of being spread evenly over whole episodes.

Composition failures: checking and repairing outcomes.

InternW0 has 761 precondition failures, 271 of them on cooking (CP04), where it switches on the heat before all ingredients are in the pot. Each step is executed, but its outcome is not checked before the next one starts. Such failures call for checking whether the required physical state has been achieved before proceeding, and repairing a step that failed. The scripted demonstrations show only steps that succeed, so a policy never sees a failed step followed by its repair. Recovery demonstrations can begin at frequently observed failures, such as a slipped grasp or an incomplete placement, and show how to restore progress.

Breakpoints: targeted data for end-to-end policies.

These diagnoses also guide data collection. Because an end-to-end policy learns its behavior from demonstrations, the cards show where new data for it should be built. On whiteboard restoration (CP09), 299 of 300 G0.5 episodes end before the board is lifted off its stand, so the later stages of the task are never reached. Adding full-length demonstrations would spend most of their steps on later stages, which the policy almost never reaches. Demonstrations constructed around the breakpoint instead, starting from the states in which episodes stop and from perturbed states near them, concentrate the training data where the policy fails.

Agents: the harness.

For agents, the same codes also point to the harness. GPT-6 Astra breaks down mostly during execution and often stops after its motion planner rejects the requested poses (Section 6.2), so finer motion tools and a retry step before stopping come first. Tool feedback should help distinguish an ineffective request from a completed operation and support an appropriate retry or alternative action. The harness can also return the outcome of each step and require a check before the next one, which addresses composition failures. It can also keep a record of earlier failures, so that an agent recognizes a breakpoint it has met before.

7 Limitations and Future Directions

7.1 Limitations

Limited causal attribution.

Each view is a set of tasks, not an intervention on one system. A Mind task still requires routine manipulation, an Act task still requires the robot to perceive its cue, and the Mind2Act workflows are longer than the single-view tasks and differ from them in content (Section 5.2). A low Mind2Act result therefore cannot yet be separated from the effect of a longer horizon or of an early execution error. The diagnosis harness attributes failures within each episode, where rules settle 22 to 38% of the failures of the three diagnosed systems and the LLM judge, with human review of uncertain cases, attributes the rest.

Paused clock and a fixed agent harness.

Simulation pauses during inference, so timed tasks test whether an action is chosen and timed correctly in simulation time, not in real time (Section 5.2). The agents also receive an inverse-kinematics and motion-planning service and four times the physics budget of the end-to-end policies, and they are not trained on the benchmark. All three agents use the same fixed harness, so the results do not show what a model would achieve with its own tools, controllers or memory. We therefore rank agents and end-to-end policies on separate leaderboards and treat the lead of the strongest agent as a result under the paused clock rather than as real-time ability.

Limited system coverage.

The results cover three agents, four VLAs and two WAMs, and they include no hybrid or memory-augmented system. This is enough to compare the two families but too few for a broader analysis, for example of how model size, training data or architecture shapes the results on Mind, Act and Mind2Act. Each agent is also evaluated on only ten episodes per task and level, so its results by difficulty level are coarse. Some episodes were run again after infrastructure failures (Appendix B).

Limited embodiments and settings.

All tasks are tabletop manipulation tasks in simulation on one bimanual platform with parallel grippers, and each task and level uses one fixed English instruction. Other embodiments and settings, such as dexterous hands, mobile manipulation, navigation and humanoid robots, are not yet covered. The Random setting changes appearance over a wide range and is not meant to model a deployment scene. Each capability category contains between one and six tasks, which is too few to support claims about a single category. How the results in simulation relate to results on the physical robot has not yet been measured.

7.2 Future Directions

We group the planned extensions into four directions that match the panels of Fig. 10, and the leaderboards will be updated with new systems, tasks and results as these extensions are added.

Composition and outcome feedback.

The current views show where a system fails, and the next step is to show why. On the Mind2Act tasks, an oracle for Mind will supply the task state that would otherwise have to be remembered or inferred, and an oracle for Act will let a system call scripted skills for the physical operations. The gain from each oracle shows how much that capability contributes, and the gap that remains with both oracles shows the cost of composition. Each Mind2Act workflow will also be paired with the Mind and Act tasks that share its demands, and progress will be reported for each stage as the share of episodes that pass it among those that reach it, which removes the effect of horizon length. Matched pairs of runs that start from the same task state and differ only in whether the system receives feedback on a grasp, a placement or a contact will then measure how much the outcome of an action guides the next decision.

Broader and fairer comparison.

The leaderboards will cover more systems and settings, so that the comparison between the two families no longer rests on one fixed setup.
