The task suite will also grow beyond tabletop bimanual manipulation to dexterous hands, mobile manipulation, navigation and humanoid robots, so that the three views can be tested on other embodiments. Human teleoperation and a scripted expert acting through each interface will give every task a reachable upper bound, and a version of the protocol that adds inference time to the simulation clock will show how much of the agents’ result on timed tasks remains in real time. A sandbox setting with its own leaderboard will let an agent bring its own harness, which runs in an isolated container with access only to the cameras, the robot state and joint-level control. The evaluated systems will extend to memory-augmented end-to-end policies, which test whether the weak memory of the VLAs comes from their architecture, and to hybrid systems that pair a language-model planner with a learned executor, which test whether combining the memory of the best agent with the practiced motions of the VLAs closes part of the gap. Repeated runs of the same instances will show how much results vary, together with the time and cost of each evaluation, and the difficulty levels of tasks on which the levels currently make no difference will be recalibrated.

From diagnosis to better models.

The diagnosis will move from explaining failures to guiding improvement. It will cover every evaluated system rather than three representative ones, and its rules and prompts will be released. The current harness reports only the first unrecoverable error of each episode, which shows where an episode breaks but not what happens after it. The diagnosis will therefore trace the whole course of a failed episode and record multiple breakpoints, including how an early error leads to later ones and whether the system notices a mistake and recovers from it. Episodes will also start from verified intermediate states of the scripted demonstrations, so that each stage of a workflow is measured even when an earlier stage fails. A developer can then change a model in response to its profile card and evaluate the new model on the same instances to check whether the change helped.

Transfer to real robots.

The last direction tests whether the findings hold outside simulation. Mind2Act World will add real-robot experiments in which its tasks are mapped to physical counterparts, starting with Mind2Act tasks such as CP02 and CP04 and extending to a wider set of tasks, so that the Mind, Act and Mind2Act results can be verified on physical hardware. The same tasks will also be paired with similar tasks in other simulators, which shows how much of the failure analysis carries across platforms.

8 Conclusion

We introduce Mind2Act World, a benchmark that measures what a robot retains and decides, how well it executes, and whether the two hold together when each physical outcome sets the next decision. Thirty tasks in three views, each with three difficulty levels and paired Clean and Random scenes, yield 180 configurations, all scored from physical outcomes by the same evaluator for agents and end-to-end policies.

Our evaluation of three agents, four VLAs, and two WAMs over 56,700 episodes yields three main findings. First, the strongest agent leads every view without task-specific training, operating under a paused clock and with a motion planner, while the four fine-tuned VLAs have similar Overall success rates and differ mainly in the tasks they handle best. Second, single-view ability does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks: the best system falls from 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act to 12.0% on Mind2Act, and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Third, the VLAs are limited even before composition, by memory that mostly disappears when the scene changes and by the first physical contact of the longer workflows. Eight of the thirty tasks are completed by no system.

Wang Yangming held that knowing and acting are one. In current embodied systems, they remain separate abilities, unevenly developed and not yet joined. Mind2Act World makes the distance between them measurable. The interventions, references and additional systems described in Section 7 are our next steps toward explaining it.

Appendix A Simulation Platform and Data Details

This appendix complements Section 4.1 with the details needed to rebuild the task scenes and to regenerate the demonstration data.

A.1 Simulation Platform

Mind2Act World runs in Isaac Sim with two ARX X5 arms and parallel grippers. A fixed head camera and two wrist cameras provide RGB images. Physics is stepped at 120 Hz and robot targets are updated at 30 Hz. Simulation pauses while a model computes, so task deadlines are measured in simulation time and cost in wall-clock time. Each task is defined by a specification that fixes the scene, the objects and mechanisms, the per-level parameters, the episode randomization and the evaluator. Changing the level or the seed changes only these parameters, never the objective or the scoring rule.

A.2 Assets and Parallel Evaluation

As shown in Fig. 6, task scenes combine shared robot and workspace assets with task-specific objects, instruments, and mechanisms. Their geometry, motion, and contact properties are configured so that every required effect is physically realized: a button travels and releases, a dial retains its reading after release, cloth stays folded only if it is laid flat, and a balance beam deflects under the actual load. Physical completion checks compare simulator states and events with task requirements, including release and support after placement.

Episodes run in isolated simulator processes. A scheduler distributes task-level conditions across the available GPUs and checks the first result of each condition before launching its remaining seeds. A valid policy failure lets evaluation continue, whereas a runtime failure blocks the remaining seeds for inspection. Model services may persist across episodes, and requests from concurrent episodes are kept apart, so that each episode observes its own visual-action sequence.

A.3 Demonstration Collection

Demonstrations are collected under one protocol for every task and level: 50 episodes per task and level for all thirty tasks (4,500 in total), all recorded in Clean scenes. Each episode records the instruction, three RGB streams at 30 Hz, and the joint states, with joint targets logged at 120 Hz. A demonstration qualifies only if the evaluator marks it successful. For timing-critical tasks it must also keep a margin, for example at least 1 s between withdrawal and gate closure in DR3. Experts are scripted: task scripts set the operation sequence and end-effector targets, and inverse kinematics and motion planning produce the joint trajectories (Section 3.4.1). Recording checks identify missing or corrupted frames, invalid state or action values, misaligned timestamps, and duplicate recordings. Together with the physical completion checks, they ensure that demonstrations show the required behavior and yield consistent training records.

A.4 Instance Generation: Clean and Random Settings

Every task and level has a frozen set of 50 evaluation slots, and each slot can be run in two settings that share the task instance and differ only in the scene around it. Each setting counts as a separate configuration, so the thirty tasks, three levels and two settings give the 180 configurations of the benchmark. Evaluation seeds are not used for training.

Clean.

The slot’s task seed draws the task-relevant parameters described in Section 3.5.1: object layouts, initial and target states, event orders and hidden parameters such as the PR5 stamp angle. Appearance is fixed to the default scene, with its table and floor materials and lighting, and no unrelated objects are present.

Random.

The same slot keeps its task seed, so objects, targets and events are identical to the clean instance. A separate environment seed adds three kinds of scene perturbation. (i) Clutter objects are drawn from a shared library and placed on free table space, and their poses are recorded after they settle under physics. (ii) Table and floor materials are drawn from a texture library. (iii) The light type is drawn from six (dome, rectangular, distant, sphere, cylinder, disk), its intensity is scaled by 0.8–1.2, and each RGB channel is scaled by 0–2. The amount of clutter is set per task and, for most tasks, does not change with the difficulty level. Clutter is placed only on free table space, never on a conveyor belt. The Random scene of a slot is fixed, so systems run on the same slot start from the same scene.

Fig. 4 gives examples of the two settings. All nine evaluated systems cover all thirty tasks in both settings. Reproducing a result requires the setting as well as the instance identifier.

Appendix B Evaluation Protocol Details

With the scenes and test instances fixed by Appendix A, this appendix specifies how a system interacts with them, expanding Section 4: what it observes and how it acts, how long an episode may run, how the episode is scored, and how results are selected.

B.1 Observations, Actions and Hidden State

A policy receives the task instruction, the selected RGB cameras with arm joint positions and the declared gripper state, and earlier public observations and permitted feedback. Hidden task state is excluded, including unannounced targets and tolerances such as the PR5 angle, the DR3 gate timing and the DR4 drift radius. The evaluator uses it only to check contact, support, timing and completion.

End-to-end policies predict joint or end-effector actions. Joint predictions are denormalized and relative offsets converted to absolute targets. Cartesian poses are transformed into the controller frame and mapped to joint targets by inverse kinematics. Each policy executes its configured chunk before predicting again. Agents instead select Cartesian targets through motion tools, which a local inverse-kinematics and motion-planning service turns into trajectories using declared robot and fixed-scene geometry. Depth and pixel-to-world queries are disabled, and agents may retrieve earlier public images without advancing the simulation. The planner, history access and any adapter fallback are therefore part of the evaluated system (Table 9).

B.2 Horizons and Budgets

The end-to-end task horizon uses the 90th percentile of demonstration duration at each level, multiplied by 1.2 and rounded up to a control step. Clean and Random share it. Agents use this physics budget multiplied by four and at most 150 decisions per episode (Table 10). Rejected and invalid actions count as decisions. Network retries do not, with up to 12 retries per decision. An agent episode ends when the task is complete, when the agent stops, or when either budget is used. Wall-clock limits are safety stops. An episode stopped by one is scored like any other unfinished episode.

B.3 Task Score

The task evaluator produces a score between 0 and 100 using the task-specific rule shown on the task pages of the project website. A successful episode scores 100. Any other outcome receives the partial credit defined for that task, or zero. For example, CP01 gives credit for each requested item released into the correct tray and remaining supported, and full success additionally requires every order to be complete and the meal trays to be retrieved. Partial-credit scales differ between tasks, so scores are compared across systems on one task and averaged within a view, but not compared across tasks.

For each task, the evaluator marks an episode as successful when it meets all completion criteria, satisfies any prerequisites, and violates no rule that prevents success. We calculate each system’s success rate by dividing the number of episodes marked as successful by the total number of evaluated episodes.

B.4 Evaluation Integrity and Result Selection

Every system on a leaderboard receives the same frozen list of task, level and seed instances. Reset restores the robot, objects, task stage, evaluator and random state, and clears policy memory. Each episode writes a manifest that binds the task, level, seed and configuration hashes to the observation profile, action interface, model or checkpoint version, clocks, budgets, termination reason and scorer output, together with an event record that separates the issued action from the evaluator’s completion check. All evaluations in this report were run by the benchmark team on its own machines.

Retained attempts.

Each system receives one result per test instance and scene setting. Infrastructure failures can trigger a retry. A valid run in which the policy fails the task still counts as a failure. Earlier attempts may remain in the logs for cost tracking, but each retained result counts only once.

Appendix C Systems and Training Details

For reproducibility, this appendix reports the initialization, global batch size and number of training steps of every evaluated end-to-end policy, the four VLAs and the two WAMs, each fine-tuned on the 4,500 demonstrations of Mind2Act World (Section 3.4.2). The three agents, GPT-6 Astra, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Gemini-4-Argon, require no training: each is called zero-shot through its API with medium reasoning effort.

G0.5. G0.5 [22] is initialized from its public pretrained checkpoint and fine-tuned with a global batch size of 240 for 136,526 steps.

π0.5\pi_{0.5}. π0.5\pi_{0.5} [20] is initialized from its public pretrained checkpoint and fine-tuned with a global batch size of 256 for 264,305 steps.

KinRT. KinRT [73] is initialized from its public pretrained checkpoint and fine-tuned with a global batch size of 256 for 264,305 steps.

X-VLA. X-VLA [74] is initialized from its public pretrained checkpoint and fine-tuned with a global batch size of 2,048 for 41,747 steps.

InternW0. The world action model InternW0 [76] is initialized from its public pretrained checkpoint and fine-tuned with a global batch size of 2,048 for 32,000 steps.

FastWAM. The world action model FastWAM [75] is initialized from its public pretrained checkpoint and fine-tuned with a global batch size of 512 for 79,210 steps.

Appendix D Detailed Results

This appendix gives the numbers behind Section 5. Table 11 reports Overall scores and success counts in each setting, Table 12 the success counts of each view with confidence intervals, Table 13 the task scores and setting-level success rates of every task, and Table 14 the successes of two end-to-end policies by difficulty level. Evaluation time and API cost are reported in Table 6.

Appendix E Diagnostic Details

This appendix defines the diagnostic steps and failure codes used in Section 6, gives the task-level results behind the per-view discussion, lists what each diagnosis layer settles for the three diagnosed systems, gives the model profile cards of three representative systems and the stop reasons of the agent episodes, and closes with the behavioral profiles.

E.1 Diagnostic Steps and Failure Codes

For each failed episode, we look for the first error from which the system could no longer recover. An error that the system later corrects does not count. We assign the failure to the earliest stage that explains the observed outcome. For example, choosing the wrong object to grasp is a reasoning error. Choosing the correct object but failing to hold it is an execution error.

We defined the failure codes by mapping the steps of each of the 30 tasks and identifying what could go wrong at each step. Table 15 lists the resulting 21 codes. Eighteen describe failures in four stages: perceiving the scene and reasoning about the next action (Mind), executing the action (Act), and checking its physical outcome to decide what to do next (Mind-Action composition). The remaining three codes apply to the episode as a whole: the system exhausts its physics or decision budget, stalls or repeats an action, or leaves too little evidence to identify the failure. These codes are not assigned to a side. Each task uses only the codes relevant to its steps. The side of a failure (Mind, Act or composition) follows from its stage, whatever the view of the task. A misread cue in an Act task counts as a Mind failure. The assignment is a classification of the first unrecoverable error and is not a causal test.

E.2 Task-Level Results by View

This section gives the task-level success counts behind the per-view discussion of Section 5.2.

Success is concentrated in a few tasks.

For three of the four VLAs, one task, passing through gates that open and close on a cycle (DR3), accounts for 36–41% of all successes: 238 of 628 for KinRT, 236 of 574 for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 227 of 626 for X-VLA. For X-VLA, three tasks (DR3, cloth folding PR4 and resistance adjustment PR1) account for 549 of its 626 successes. Gemini-4-Argon shows the same pattern on a smaller scale: resistance adjustment and gate passage together contribute 24 of its 42 successes.

Eight tasks are completed by no system.

Workpiece tracking (M1), tray carrying with loose balls (DR4), oriented stamping (PR5), the domino chain (PR6), moving-rack loading (CP03), temperature-controlled cooking (CP04), bridge building (CP07) and whiteboard restoration (CP09) have no successful episode among the 56,700. On four of them (DR4, PR6, CP07 and CP09), every system also has a mean task score of zero, meaning that not even the first scored stage is reached. Each of these tasks has fifty scripted demonstrations per level that pass the same evaluator, confirming platform feasibility.

Mind

End-to-end policies.

The VLAs complete few Mind episodes, and their successes are concentrated in a narrow set of tasks. KinRT’s 132 Mind successes include 46 on steamer-stack restoration (P2), 22 on card matching (M2), and 20 on repeated-item recognition (E1). Of the 105 successes of π0.5\pi_{0.5}, 43 are on P2 and 22 on hazard navigation (S2). These successes occur mostly at the Easy level, where the least information must be retained (Table 14 for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and G0.5), and mostly in Clean scenes (Section 5.2). Across the four VLAs, workpiece tracking (M1) is never completed and tray-layout restoration (S1) only once. A policy that conditions on the current observation or on a short history cannot recover information that has left its view, and the Mind results of the VLAs are consistent with this limitation. Evaluating memory-augmented policies [29, 30, 56] on the Mind view provides a direct test.

Agents.

GPT-6 Astra succeeds in 52.7% of Mind episodes, but its performance is uneven within three of the five categories: 100% on hazard navigation (S2) against 23.3% on tray-layout restoration (S1), 93.3% on card matching (M2) against 0% on workpiece tracking (M1), and 43.3% on meal orders (P1) against 0% on steamer-stack restoration (P2). The tasks it solves best are those in which the action is a button press or a simple placement (S2, F1, M2, E2, E1), whereas the tasks it fails additionally require lifting covers, routing a workpiece through stations, or unstacking and restacking baskets. Its Mind score therefore reflects the reach of its motion tools as well as its memory, and because each category contains only two tasks, category-level differences should not be read as differences between kinds of memory. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash shows the same pattern on a smaller scale: its 33 Mind successes all come from five of these tasks (M2 10, E1 6, E2 6, S2 6 and F1 5). Gemini-4-Argon obtains its 13 on six tasks.

Act

End-to-end policies.

Act is the view in which the VLAs succeed most often, and their success comes mainly from dynamic response. Averaged over tasks, the four VLAs reach 22–28% on the four dynamic tasks and 4–18% on the six precision tasks. Although they are trained on the same demonstration collection, the policies differ sharply from task to task, and no single policy leads throughout: G0.5 leads on DR1 and DR2, KinRT on DR3, and X-VLA on PR1 and PR4. G0.5 leads light-cued response (DR2, 110 of 300 episodes) but is last on resistance adjustment (PR1, 9), where X-VLA leads with 130. X-VLA also completes 192 cloth-folding episodes (PR4), against 30 to 54 for the other three. Apart from the zero-success tasks DR4, PR5 and PR6, pen tracing (PR3) is completed only three times in 1,200 VLA episodes.

Agents.

GPT-6 Astra completes every resistance-adjustment episode and most episodes of the three timed tasks DR1, DR2, and DR3 (76.7%, 90.0%, and 80.0%), yet it completes no episode of the five tasks that require continuous contact or a carried load (DR4, PR3, PR4, PR5, and PR6). The Hard level of DR2 allows 2.6 s to press a lit button, whereas the agent’s mean request time on Act tasks is 9.2 s. Because simulation pauses during inference, the agent can still meet the deadline. These results show that the agent selects and times actions correctly in simulation time. They do not test real-time reaction.

Mind2Act

Table 16 lists the completed Mind2Act episodes of every system by task.

The composition gap of the strongest system.

GPT-6 Astra succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes. If a Mind2Act workflow required one independent success of each kind, 20.5% of its Mind2Act episodes would succeed. It completes only 12.0% (36 of 300, 95% Wilson interval [8.8, 16.2]%). Eighteen of the 36 successes come from conveyor meal assembly (CP01), and it completes none of CP03, CP04, CP07, CP09 or CP10. The two weaker agents complete no Mind2Act episode, which gives a 95% Wilson interval of [0, 1.3]% for each of their success rates.

For the VLAs, composition is not the first bottleneck.

The VLAs complete 0.2–3.6% of Mind2Act episodes, close to their Mind success rates (1.0–4.4%) and far below their Act rates. For KinRT, π0.5\pi_{0.5} and G0.5, the Mind2Act rate exceeds the product of the Mind and Act rates (for example, 3.6% against 0.4% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}), and for X-VLA the two are about equal (0.2%). This reflects concentration: produce weighing (CP06) and conveyor meal assembly (CP01) supply 75 of KinRT’s 88 Mind2Act successes, 88 of the 109 of π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and 61 of the 69 of G0.5, mostly at the Easy level. At Easy, CP01 has a single order and CP06 a single item to weigh, so little must be remembered and a practiced motion carries most of the task. For these policies, the two workflows then behave much like Act tasks. InternW0 departs from this pattern: block structure from a shown blueprint (CP08) contributes 35 of its 91 Mind2Act successes, more than any other end-to-end policy completes on that task, while produce weighing (CP06) contributes 48.

Mind2Act workflows mostly fail early.

On the four workflows that no system completes (CP03, CP04, CP07 and CP09), the mean task score of every system is at most 1.2 points out of 100. The profile card of G0.5 (Fig. 12) shows why for one policy: 202 of its 300 bridge-building episodes (CP07) never grasp a piece. Elsewhere, partial credit adds little. For every system, the Mind2Act score exceeds the success rate by at most 1.5 points, so under the current scoring rules a failed Mind2Act episode has usually failed early rather than near completion. For most systems evaluated here, these four workflows therefore end at the first physical step, before the composition they were designed to test. InternW0 on cooking (CP04) is the exception: in 271 of its 300 episodes it switches on the heat before all ingredients are in the pot, which is a composition error.

What the view-level comparison shows.

Conveyor meal assembly (CP01) reuses the conveyor interception of DR1 and, like P1, depends on remembered food orders. Yet GPT-6 Astra completes CP01 more often (60.0%) than P1 (43.3%), and every VLA that completes any CP01 episode does so more often than the product of its P1 and DR1 rates would predict (8.0% for KinRT against 0.1%). A Mind2Act task is thus not simply the conjunction of two single-view tasks, and a lower Mind2Act score cannot by itself be attributed to composition. The views instead show a narrower finding: each system’s ability is uneven across Mind and Act, the systems differ in which is weaker, and every system succeeds less often on the Mind2Act workflows than on its stronger single view.

E.3 What Each Diagnosis Layer Settles

Table 17 lists, for the three systems of Appendix E.4, how many failed episodes the rule layer settles and how many pass to the LLM judge. Where the judge is uncertain whether the evidence decides the first unrecoverable step, or where repeated judge calls disagree, human reviewers settle the code. The lower block compares the attribution of the rule-settled failures with that of all failures. For the two end-to-end policies the rule layer attributes more failures to the Mind side than to any other, because scorer records reveal a misremembered item more readily than video reveals a motor fault. Over all failures, execution errors are the largest group.

E.4 Model Profile Cards of Three System Types

Figs. 12–14 give the model profile cards of G0.5, InternW0 and GPT-6 Astra, one representative system of each evaluated type (a VLA, a WAM and an agent), in the format of Fig. 9. Unlike the examples in Figs. 8 and 9, these cards report measured results. The success rates are those of Table 4. The failure panels cover every failed episode: 8,470 for G0.5, 8,220 for InternW0 and 589 for GPT-6 Astra. Rules settle the episodes they can decide, the judge reviews the rest, and human reviewers settle the cases the judge marks as uncertain (Section 6.1).

Reading the three cards.

The two end-to-end policies share a profile but break in different ways. G0.5 most often fails to grasp or hold an object (1,324 episodes) and stalls in 866 episodes. In repeated-item recognition (E1), 250 of its 300 episodes stop before the batch is submitted. InternW0 stalls less, but in 761 episodes it proceeds before a precondition holds: in 271 of its 300 cooking episodes (CP04), it switches on the heat before all recipe ingredients are in the pot. Fine-control errors are its most frequent code (1,132 episodes), and it misapplies the keypad rule in 288 of 299 failed episodes of E2. GPT-6 Astra fails mostly on the execution side (55% of its failures, against 30% on the Mind side), led by grasp (120) and fine-control errors (107): every tray-carrying episode (DR4) is lost during the lift, and 21 of 30 domino-chain episodes (PR6) end with pieces knocked over while they are placed. The cards therefore point to different remedies: grasp demonstrations and task-state memory for G0.5, contact-rich demonstrations and precondition checks for InternW0, and finer motion tools with a check-and-retry step before stopping for the agent.

E.5 Stop Reasons of Agent Episodes

Table 18 gives the reasons for which the episodes of the three agents ended, as used in Section 6.2. A stop by the agent is its own decision to end the episode. The completion flag is set by the environment, not by the agent. It records how the episode ended and does not imply a full score, which comes from the task evaluator. The two budget rows count episodes that reach the limit of 150 decisions or of simulated time. The stop reasons are read from the termination field of each retained episode result. On average, an episode uses 79.6 decisions for GPT-6 Astra, 111.8 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and about 33 for Gemini-4-Argon.

E.6 Behavioral Profiles, Just for Fun

Each model profile card also carries a four-letter behavioral profile, such as the ENFP of Fig. 9. It borrows the MBTI format to turn four comparisons of success rates into a code that is easy to remember and share. Each letter asks one MBTI-style question of a robot policy and answers it with two task groups of the benchmark (Table 19). The system takes the letter of the group on which it succeeds more often, so every profile has four letters. Where the two rates differ by less than one percentage point (G0.5’s N and P), the card keeps the letter and marks the lean as weak. A profile says how a system tends to succeed and fail, not how well it performs. The numbers behind it are in the quantitative sections of the card.

How the letters are borrowed.

Each MBTI dimension is matched to the closest contrast in the benchmark. For example, extraverts get things done out in the world and introverts think things over, so a policy that does better on Act is an E and one that does better on Mind is an I. The other three letters follow Table 19 in the same way. The information letter uses only entity memory (E1, E2) and spatial memory (S1, S2). The other Mind categories mix several kinds of memory and stay out of the letters.

As in MBTI, the first and last letters sort the codes into four families. Feedforward Planners (I ·· J) think more than they do and stick to a plan made in advance. Feedback Adapters (I ·· P) think more than they do and correct course step by step. Procedural Executors (E ·· J) do more than they think and follow a fixed routine. Servo Responders (E ·· P) have steady hands that adjust as the scene changes. The middle letters add the details: what the system remembers better (S or N) and whether its hands are more accurate (T) or more timely (F). Since every end-to-end policy evaluated here succeeds more often on Act than on Mind (Table 4), all of them start with E, while GPT-6 Astra starts with I.

Meet the three diagnosed systems.

InternW0 is an ENFP, a Goalkeeper among the Servo Responders, and holds all four letters firmly: it succeeds more often on Act than on Mind (17.6% against 5.4%), on spatial than on entity memory (5.3% against 0.2%), on dynamic response than on precise execution (31.8% against 8.1%), and on feedback-driven than on plan-driven workflows (5.6% against 0.5%). G0.5 is an ENFP too, though only just on the memory and lifestyle letters (0.0% against 0.8%, and 2.1% against 2.5%). GPT-6 Astra is an ISFJ, a Dispatcher among the Feedforward Planners: Mind-led (52.7% against 39.0% on Act), better at entity than spatial memory (68.3% against 61.7%), more successful on dynamic response than on precise execution (61.7% against 23.9%, though its F says only that the timed tasks go better than the precision tasks, not that it reacts fast), and better on plan-driven than on feedback-driven workflows (16.0% against 8.0%). In short, the two Goalkeepers do relatively best on dynamic response, and the Dispatcher completes plan-driven workflows twice as often as feedback-driven ones.

Appendix F Task Details

This appendix is the reference for the tasks. It explains where they come from, what each one asks, and how it gets harder. Mind tasks emphasize retaining information and selecting actions, Act tasks emphasize physical precision and timely response, and Mind2Act tasks combine remembered or inferred task state with execution outcomes that constrain subsequent actions. Table 20 lists all thirty tasks. Every task has 50 demonstrations per level (4,500 in total) and is covered by all nine evaluated systems (Table 5).

The three levels describe changes in task demands rather than a calibrated difficulty ranking. Demonstration and evaluation seeds are disjoint. The common observation and scoring protocol in Section 4 applies throughout.

F.1 From Real-World Requirements to Tasks

Each task is built from a requirement that makes a real activity hard for a robot. Table 20 names, for every task, the real-world source it is built from, its capability category (for Mind2Act, the demand pairing) and the variables raised with difficulty. Fig. 16 groups the same tasks into the five application domains of Table 2.

F.2 Task Cards

Each card shows four frames from one expert recording. The frames illustrate the task and may come from a lower level than the listed instruction. The card also gives the English instruction as stored in the demonstrations (the Hard-level text where the levels differ, with a per-episode target inserted in PR1 and PR2), the condition for final success, and the Easy/Medium/Hard configuration. The category follows Section 3. Success is evaluated on simulator states and events, some of them checked throughout the episode. A note in parentheses gives events that are irreversible or unscored. Every task is used for both training and evaluation, with 50 demonstrations per task and level (Section 3.4.2). The score values of each task and level are listed on the task pages of the project website.

Mind tasks

Ten tasks that test memory and reasoning with routine execution.

 

E1 Repeated-item recognition Entity memory

Instruction. Hard: Observe and remember each batch of items. After the first batch, place the one item that appeared in any of the previous five batches into the submission tray.

Success. Every repeated item stably deposited in its submission tray (first batch is observation-only).

E / M / H. 3/5/7 batches, 4/4/6 objects per batch and 2/4/6 submissions. Repeats come from the previous 1, up to 3, or up to 5 batches.

 

E2 Object-coded keypad arithmetic Entity memory

Instruction. Observe the visible entity-value associations, remember them, decode the physical expression, and enter its exact result using only the closed gripper fingertips on the nine keys.

Success. All digits of the exact result entered in order after effective press-release, with no wrong, missing or extra press.

E / M / H. 3/4/6 object-value bindings shown, then hidden; the board then shows an arithmetic expression over the same objects (Medium and Hard repeat objects), whose result is typed on keys 1–9.

 

F1 Unknown button mapping Feedback-rule learning

Instruction. Hard: Probe the four unmarked buttons and remember how each moves the slider. After the slider resets and the goal appears, reach the visible goal on the 4 by 4 grid using the fewest presses.

Success. Slider reaches the visible goal after the slider reset. A held button does not retrigger, and out-of-bounds input has no effect.

E / M / H. A linear track, a 3 by 3 grid, or a 4 by 4 grid, with 2/4/4 buttons. Shortest routes are 1–3/2–3/4–6 steps. Exploration cost is recorded separately.

 

F2 Color-block arrangement by feedback Feedback-rule learning

Instruction. Place one colored block in each slot, then press and release the confirmation button on the right. The brief feedback gives the number of correct positions. Infer the hidden permutation in as few attempts as possible.

Success. Correct arrangement found within the submission budget: one released, supported block per slot, stable ≥\geq0.5 s, then button released (press on an incomplete layout is not a submission).

E / M / H. 3/4/5 blocks and slots; 5/6/7 valid submissions.

 

P1 Incremental meal orders Process memory

Instruction. Hard: Remember the initial orders and two additional orders shown later. Place all requested ingredients into the indicated containers; each additional order adds to earlier demand.

Success. Each container holds exactly the requested types and quantities.

E / M / H. 2/2/3 containers and 4/5/7 deposits. All levels start with two orders requesting four items. Later additions are none, one order adding one item, or two orders adding two and one items.

 

P2 Steamer-stack order restoration Process memory

Instruction. Hard: Remove the lid, remember the dim sum order as you unstack the baskets from top to bottom onto the mats, then restack them in the same order from bottom to top on the left steamer pot and replace the lid without using any distractor baskets.

Success. Correct original baskets restacked in original order on the left pot, stable, lid placed; the final stack holds no extra basket (setting one aside temporarily is allowed).

E / M / H. 3/4/4 layers to restore; 0/0/2 distractor baskets that look the same outside but hold different dumplings.

 

S1 Tray-layout restoration Spatial memory

Instruction. Remember the four colored slots, observe the carousel rotation, then place each colored block into its original matching slot after the carousel stops.

Success. All four blocks in their original tray-relative cells.

E / M / H. 1–2 slow rotation segments in one direction, 3–4 segments with reversals, or 5–6 faster segments with repeated reversals. All levels use four colors, four placements and the same placement tolerances.

 

S2 Hidden-hazard navigation Spatial memory

Instruction. Remember the briefly lit forbidden cells. Press and release the arrow buttons to move one cell per press. Reach the ring without entering a forbidden cell or leaving the board. Do not touch the slider.

Success. Slider supported and inside the board throughout, never touching a hazard, fully in the goal and stable ≥\geq0.5 s (any hazard contact or leaving the board precludes success).

E / M / H. 4×44\times 4/5×55\times 5/6×66\times 6 boards with 3/7/12 hazard cells; shortest routes of 6/10/14 steps in the first instance.

 

M1 Workpiece tracking and route replay Integrated memory

Instruction. Remember the target location and station route. Track the target through the cover exchanges, uncover it, and move it through the required stations in order.

Success. Target retrieved and initial station plus visits replayed in order, each placement released and stable (temporary tabletop placements do not count).

E / M / H. 4/4/6 stations and 3/5/7 exchanges, including 0/1/2 exchanges unrelated to the target. Replay requires 4/5/6 placements. Medium and Hard include at least one and two revisits, respectively.

 

M2 Card-matching game Integrated memory

Instruction. Press and release a card’s yellow button to turn it face up, revealing at most two unmatched cards at a time. Matching pictures stay face up; mismatches turn face down automatically. Wait until the flip or pair result finishes before selecting another card. Remember the pictures and their positions and match every pair.

Success. All pairs matched and held face-up (mismatches are exploration, not failure).

E / M / H. 2×22\times 2/2×42\times 4/4×44\times 4 layouts with 2/4/8 pairs.

Act tasks

Ten tasks that test timing and precision, with the operation stated in the instruction.

 

DR1 Conveyor pickup Dynamic response

Instruction. Hard: Pick up all 7 packages on the conveyor belt and place them in the central collection tray.

Success. All required packages stably deposited within budget, none missed (a package that leaves the reach region counts as missed).

E / M / H. 3/5/7 packages arrive on the conveyor, and all of them must be collected into the central tray.

 

DR2 Light-cued response Dynamic response

Instruction. Hard: Press the currently illuminated button within 2.6 seconds and release within 1 second. Respond correctly to all 10 cues; never press an unlit button.

Success. Ten correct press-release events, each released within 1 s. A repeated cue needs a separate event.

E / M / H. Cue-to-press deadlines are 4.0/3.2/2.6 s. Button geometry, ten-cue count and release timing stay fixed.

 

DR3 Timed passage through cyclic gates Dynamic response

Instruction. Hard: Grasp the eraser, time the moving gates, and pass through the blue then the orange opening to place the eraser stably in the green tray behind them. Withdraw the whole gripper past the outer gate before they close. Do not touch any gate, frame or rail.

Success. The eraser is carried through each open gate in order and left supported in the tray. Dropping or throwing it into the tray earns only the gate-passage credit. When a gate first closes after the eraser has passed, both arms must be clear of its passage on the near side (arm contact with a gate, frame or rail during that closure precludes success).

E / M / H. One gate fully open for 6.6/6.0 s per 11.2/10.6 s cycle on Easy/Medium; on Hard, two gates with 18.4 s and 9.2 s cycles whose shared openings alternate between 3.6 s, too short for the measured 5.1 s action chain, and 6.4 s.

 

DR4 Tray carrying with loose balls Dynamic response (stability)

Instruction. Hard: Carry the tray of four balls by its handle from START to DESTINATION around the two staggered columns, keeping each ball inside its marked circle. Set the tray down stably, release it and retreat. Do not touch the balls or hit anything.

Success. All balls stay on the tray and inside their circles throughout; tray delivered within 20 mm, vertical error <<3 mm, released, stable for the last 2 s (a ball leaving its circle, with 0.5 mm tolerance, is a latched failure).

E / M / H. 2/3/4 balls, 0/1/2 pillars, and allowed drift radii of 30/25/20 mm.

 

PR1 Resistance adjustment Precise execution

Instruction. Adjust the resistance between the left terminal and wiper to RR Ω\Omega, then release the slider and keep that reading for 0.5 seconds. (RR per episode.)

Success. Reading within ±\pm0.2/0.15/0.12 Ω\Omega, held for 0.5 s after release.

E / M / H. One target per episode on a numbered major tick, an unnumbered minor tick, or between minor ticks: 7/21/21 distinct targets, e.g. 10/16/35.75 Ω\Omega.

 

PR2 Voltage setting Precise execution

Instruction. Adjust the output voltage to VV V, then release the knob and keep that reading for 1 second. (VV per episode.)

Success. Reading within ±\pm1/0.5/0.5 V for 1 s after release.

E / M / H. One target per episode on a numbered major tick, an unnumbered minor tick, or between minor ticks: 12/33/33 distinct targets, e.g. 160/165/147 V.

 

PR3 Pen tracing Precise execution

Instruction. Grasp the marker and trace the complete visible path, then lift.

Success. At least 98% of the reference path lies within 3 mm of ink and the RMS distance from the ink to the path is at most 2 mm. Only ink from actual contact counts.

E / M / H. A straight line, an S curve with two half-waves, or a curve with four half-waves. All paths are 350 mm long with ±3\pm 3 mm centerline tolerance. Curved paths have minimum radii of about 54/25 mm.

 

PR4 Cloth folding and flat placement Precise execution

Instruction. Hard: Fold the hexagonal cloth once into the displayed trapezoid, align its paired edges, release it fully and leave it stable.

Success. Required fold made, layers and corners aligned within tolerance, inside the target frame, released and lying flat and stable.

E / M / H. Midline fold into a two-layer rectangle; diagonal fold into a two-layer triangle; a single fold of a hexagon along its symmetry axis into a two-layer trapezoid. All pieces have the same area (400 cm2), mass, and material.

 

PR5 Oriented stamping Precise execution

Instruction. Pick up square stamp A and stamp once, fully inside the blue box, with its arrow aligned to the target arrow. Do not drag or stamp twice. Return the stamp to its holder in its original orientation and release it.

Success. Exactly one imprint with all four rotated corners inside the frame and arrow within tolerance, no smear; stamp returned, gripper withdrawn. The arrow defines the orientation over the full 360°.

E / M / H. Frames of 100/80/74 mm and orientation tolerances of ±5∘\pm 5^{\circ}/±2∘\pm 2^{\circ}/±1∘\pm 1^{\circ}; targets sampled from 8/32/320 directions; minimum centered margins of 14.6/4.6/1.6 mm.

 

PR6 Domino chain to a bell Precise execution

Instruction. Stand the dominos anywhere inside the continuous curve band, in order along the curve. Push the first one so the chain of contacts rings the bell. Repair fallen or stalled segments using as few pushes as possible.

Success. Dominoes released and held in the same valid order for 0.5 s, the first one pushed, and the chain falling along the band to strike the bell.

E / M / H. 5/7/9 dominoes; heights of 10.24 (uniform)/8.32–12.00/7.68–13.44 cm; band spans of 41.3/57.3/76.1 cm.

Mind2Act tasks

Ten tasks that combine remembered state and physical outcomes in one loop.

 

CP01 Conveyor meal assembly Cumulative progress

Instruction. At the start, watch the reference meal trays pass on the conveyor and remember the three food types on each. Then prepare the corresponding empty meal trays on the table and fill each with the same three food types from the continuously moving supply.

Success. All requested foods stably in the correct meal trays; Medium and Hard also require the meal trays retrieved from the stack (no recirculation or replacement supply).

E / M / H. 1/2/3 orders with 3/6/9 food items. Easy provides one meal tray. Medium and Hard require retrieving 2 and 3 meal trays from the left stack, respectively. Belt speed remains 0.025 m/s across all levels.

 

CP02 Rotating-cake decoration Prerequisites and repair

Instruction. Hard: Remember each macaron and its place on the still cake shown for three seconds. Open the ingredient-box lid, press the green button and recreate the arrangement as the cake rotates. Then press the red button, wait for the cake to stop, and place the cake cover over it.

Success. Full layout placed and all preparation and cleanup steps done; Hard also requires the turntable stopped and at rest before the cover is placed.

E / M / H. 4/6/6 macarons at speeds of 12/20/28∘12/20/28^{\circ}/s. Easy starts open and running. Medium and Hard add opening the box lid and pressing the green button. Hard also adds the stopping and covering sequence.

 

CP03 Moving-rack loading Cumulative progress

Instruction. Hard: Load 7 upright plates into the moving empty slots without disturbing other plates. Tilt the lever fully toward the back of the machine, away from the robot, release it, then press the green button before loading.

Success. Every plate supported by both side supports and the base, earlier plates undisturbed.

E / M / H. 3/5/7 plates at 12/16/20 mm/s. All levels start with the green button; Medium first sets the lever upright in the middle, Hard tilts it fully back. Support gaps are approximately 36.5/30.5/26.5 mm. Hard reverses direction with a 0.6 s end transition while insertions occur at cruise speed.

 

CP04 Temperature-controlled cooking Feedback-driven adjustment

Instruction. Hard: Open the drawer. Pour each required jar into the pot in the remembered recipe order, returning jars upright and caps to the tray, then cover the pot. Turn the black knob to HEAT and press the green button; within 2 s after 80 °C, switch to KEEP WARM, then press it again.

Success. Ingredients added in remembered order before HEAT, KEEP WARM selected within the window before shutdown, and jars and caps returned; Medium and Hard also require the drawer opened and the pot covered.

E / M / H. 2/2/3 ordered ingredients from four jars, and HEAT must be switched to KEEP WARM within 4/3/2 s after the pot reaches 80 °C (green band up to 90/87.5/85 °C). All levels return the jars upright and their caps to the tray; Medium and Hard add opening the drawer and covering the pot. Geometric tolerances remain unchanged.

 

CP05 Piano replay Sequence and plan execution

Instruction. Hard: Set volume to MAX and release the slider. Pick up both side mallets, press the triangle-marked button and watch the demonstration while holding both, then reproduce the twelve key presses in order using either mallet. Return and release both mallets, release all keys, withdraw your arms, and keep volume at MAX.

Success. Effective strikes in the remembered sequence (rhythm need not match), mallets returned and arms withdrawn; Hard also requires the volume kept at MAX.

E / M / H. 7/14/21 candidate keys, 8/8/12 events and 1/2/2 mallets. Easy uses the central mallet; Medium and Hard pick up and return both side mallets together, and Hard also sets the volume slider from MIN to MAX and keeps it there. Either mallet may strike.

 

CP06 Produce weighing on a balance Feedback-driven adjustment

Instruction. Hard: With the empty scale stable, press ZERO. Move all fruit and vegetables from the left tray onto the left scale pan. Balance the scale using the weights on the right and by physically moving the sliding weight, then release them and keep the pointer in the green zone.

Success. All produce on the left pan, the weights needed for balance on the right pan, nothing dropped, and the pointer inside the green zone and stable for 1 s; Medium and Hard also require ZERO pressed on the empty scale, and Hard the sliding weight at its target position.

E / M / H. 1/2/3 produce items; Medium and Hard first press ZERO on the empty scale; weight sets of 2×50+2×1002\times 50{+}2\times 100 g/50–400 g/50–400 g, with a 0–40 g sliding weight added on Hard; green zones of ±10\pm 10/±8\pm 8/±5\pm 5 g; 9/16/80 candidate states, with a unique solution on Hard.

 

CP07 Bridge building for a toy car Sequence and plan execution

Instruction. Hard: Build a stable bridge across the gap with continuous wheel paths on both sides. Choose suitable pieces by shape and size from the stock, which includes extra blocks, and leave unused blocks aside. Release the bridge pieces, then press and release the button and let the car drive across to the opposite bank.

Success. Piers, caps and deck stably in place, button triggered, car upright and across the finish (unused distractor stock allowed).

E / M / H. River widths of 18/28/36 cm; 1 pier and 2 spans/2 piers and 3 spans/2 unequal piers, sloped spans, and U-shaped ramp supports; stock of 8/18/28 pieces, of which 8/13/13 are needed.

 

CP08 Block structure from a shown blueprint Prerequisites and repair

Instruction. Hard: Remember the briefly shown front view, then build the structure from memory, centred in the marked area and aligned with the table reference line. If the base is misplaced, move the beam above it aside and rebuild; put the roof ridge-up on the cylinders. Use only reference-colour blocks and release everything.

Success. Colors, shapes, positions, orientation and support match the blueprint; beam and roof each borne by two blocks; stable 1 s (Hard 5 s) after release (holding the structure up does not count; 90∘90^{\circ} roof error rejected).

E / M / H. 3 cuboids in 2 layers/3 cuboids and 1 cylinder in 3 layers/6 blocks in 4 layers with a prism roof; 0/1/2 distractors; 6/4/4 mm tolerance; 1/1/5 s hold after release.

 

CP09 Whiteboard restoration Prerequisites and repair

Instruction. Hard: Remember the briefly shown original drawing on the whiteboard. Erase the added strokes, uncap the pens of the colors needed, and redraw any original strokes you erased, so the board matches the original.

Success. Final board matches the original in color, shape and layout: extra strokes removed, over-erased parts redrawn; Medium/Hard include uncapping.

E / M / H. 2/3/4 original elements in 1/2/3 colors; added strokes of one line/a long and a short crossing line/two long lines and an extra circle. The board starts on a raised stand; the reference procedure first lays it flat on the table, though only the final board is scored.

 

CP10 Return or dodge incoming balls Predictive decision

Instruction. Predict each ball from the launcher’s settled aim. After two practice balls, use the sliding blocker to return every white ball to the far net and let every red ball pass untouched into the near net. Wait for each ball to settle before the next shot.

Success. Every scored ball correct: white returned to the far net, red cleared into the near net (two practice balls unscored).

E / M / H. 5/8/12 scored balls, of which 2/4/6 are red; shots (direct/single-bounce/double-bounce) of 3/2/0 on Easy, 2/4/2 on Medium and 2/5/5 on Hard; countdowns of 4/3/2 s.
